These formatting features build directly on the basic table structure (rows, columns, cells) introduced in the previous concept node. Proper formatting transforms a raw grid into a clear, professional‑looking information display, essential for timetables, mark sheets, and simple reports.
steps: Formatting a table with borders, shading, alignment, and merged cells makes data easy to read and looks professional.
Here is why: first, borders act like the lines on a notebook page, separating each piece of information so the eye can follow rows and columns without confusion.
Second, shading the header row — like highlighting the top of a marks card — instantly tells the reader which column means what.
Third, alignment ensures numbers line up at the right edge and titles sit centred, just as a teacher aligns roll numbers in a register.
Fourth, merging cells lets you write a single title across several columns, such as “Term 1 Exams” spanning Math, Science, and English.
Fifth, table styles give a ready‑made professional look that you can then fine‑tune.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “manually set each border and shading one by one”) reveals the misconception that table styles are only decorative and not a productivity tool — students may think they must format every element separately.
remember: What is the quickest way to apply a consistent set of borders, shading, and fonts to an entire table in one step.
If you merge two adjacent cells in a row that already contain text, what happens to the text originally in the second cell.
Evaluate the statement: “Applying shading to a table header row is only for decoration and does not improve readability.”.

cards.title: A table in a word processor is a structured grid of rows and columns used to…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A table in a word processor is a structured grid of rows and columns used to organise textual or numeric data. Each intersection of a row and column forms a cell that can hold text, numbers, or even nested tables. Core operations include inserting a table with a specified number of rows and columns, adding or deleting rows and columns after creation, merging adjacent cells to create headings that span multiple columns or rows, and splitting merged cells back into individual units. Formatting tools let users apply borders (solid, dashed, double), shading (solid colours or patterns), and predefined table styles that combine fonts, colours, and banded rows for quick professional appearance. Data manipulation features such as sorting (ascending or descending on any column) and converting the table to plain text (using tabs, commas, or other delimiters) extend the table’s utility beyond static layout. Tables relate to earlier concepts of paragraph formatting, page margins, and text alignment because they inherit the document’s default font and paragraph settings while providing a distinct layout container. Mastery of tables enables clear presentation of schedules, comparison charts, mark sheets, and any tabular information required in school projects or examinations.
steps: The key to mastering tables in a word processor is to treat each table as a flexible grid that you can shape, style, and reorganise just like a school timetable.
First, tables organise data in rows and columns, giving each piece of information a fixed address.
Second, formatting tools such as borders and shading let you highlight important rows — for example, a header row in bright saffron makes a class schedule instantly readable.
Third, merging and splitting cells adapt the grid to complex layouts, like a cricket scorecard where “Team A” spans three columns.
Fourth, sorting and conversion extend the table’s usefulness beyond static display, allowing you to reorder a mark list or export data for a spreadsheet.
Consider a Class 6 project on “Weekly Fruit Stock”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Home tab”) reveals the misconception that all formatting tools live on Home, confusing text formatting with object insertion.
remember: Which tab in a typical word processor contains the command to insert a table.
If you merge the top two cells of a 3‑column table, how many cells will the first row have.
A student applies a thick red border to the entire table and then applies a light blue shading to the header row. Will the header row’s shading be visible? Explain.

cards.title: The chapter “Word Processor” introduces students to the core functions of a…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: The chapter “Word Processor” introduces students to the core functions of a word processing application such as Microsoft Word or LibreOffice Writer. It covers the interface components — ribbon, ruler, status bar — and fundamental operations: creating, opening, saving, and printing documents. Text formatting (font, size, colour, alignment), paragraph formatting (indents, spacing, bullets), and page layout (margins, orientation, headers/footers) are explained. The chapter then progresses to advanced features: inserting tables, images, shapes, and using spell check. The culminating topic is Mail Merge, a powerful automation tool that combines a main document with a data source (e.g., an Excel sheet or CSV file) to produce personalized letters, labels, or envelopes in bulk. Understanding the relationship between the main document (template), the data source (recipient list), and the merge fields (placeholders) is essential. The chapter emphasizes why word processors are indispensable for school projects, office correspondence, and personal communication, linking each skill to real‑world tasks like writing reports, designing certificates, or sending festival invitations.
steps: The chapter gives you a toolkit to turn ideas into polished documents and then multiply them effortlessly with Mail Merge.

Here is why: first, knowing the interface lets you find any command quickly; second, formatting skills make documents readable and professional; third, page layout controls ensure printouts match expectations; fourth…
Consider you are the class monitor preparing the annual day invitation.
You open the word processor, see the ribbon tabs (Home, Insert, Layout, References, Mailings), and start a new blank document.
You type the invitation text, apply a festive font, centre the heading, add a school logo from Insert → Pictures, and set narrow margins for a compact card.
After proofreading with the spell checker, you save the file as “Invitation.docx”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Home tab”) reveals the misconception that formatting and mail merge share the same tab, confusing text styling with automation features.
remember: Which tab in a typical word processor ribbon contains the Mail Merge commands.
Explain why a data source is necessary for Mail Merge.
Evaluate the claim: “Mail Merge can only be used for printing letters.”.

cards.title: Mail merge is the word-processor feature that assembles many personalised…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Mail merge is the word-processor feature that assembles many personalised documents by combining exactly two prepared components at run time. The main document is the fixed component: it carries every word, line and layout that is identical in all copies — the letterhead, the body, the closing — together with merge fields, the marked slots that name which changing detail belongs at that position. The data source is the changing component: a grid whose fields (columns) are the categories of detail (Name, Class_Section, City) and whose records (rows) hold one complete set of values per recipient. The assembly itself is the merge run: the word processor takes the first record, copies its values into the matching merge fields, and emits a finished copy; then the second record; and so on, until every record has produced exactly one copy. One record in, one document out — the count of merged copies always equals the count of records. The merge field is the bridge between the two components, and it works by NAME, not by position: a slot marked «Name» does not mean "the first column" but "the column called Name". This is why the data source's first row must hold the field names — it is the dictionary the merge reads. The chapter's remaining nodes build each part: the list, the letter and its slots, the run and its outputs, the envelope and label variants, and the professional rules that keep a merge correct.
steps: The takeaway first: mail merge is a fixed letter joined to a moving list by named slots — the main document supplies what never changes, the data source supplies what always changes, and the merge fields tell the merge…
Supporting arguments: 1.
The separation is the design.
Every mail-merge question is secretly a classification question: "Dear Sir or Madam, the Annual Day function of our school..." belongs to the main document;
"Diya Menon, 6B, Peepal" belongs to the data source; «Student_Name» belongs in the main document as a slot.
A student who can sort any fragment into its component has understood mail merge; a student who cannot has only heard of it. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., defining a record as "one column of the list") reveals the field-record mix-up — the classic vocabulary slip; fields run down (columns), records run across (rows), and every CISCE answer is graded on that orientation.
remember: Recall: Define each of the five key terms of mail merge — main document, data source, field, record, merge field — in one sentence each.
Reasoning: A merge field is linked to its value by NAME, not by….
Evaluate: A student claims: "Since the merge run fills the slots automatically, the main document does not need proofreading — only the data source does, because the list holds….

cards.title: Mail Merge is a word‑processor feature that combines a main document
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Mail Merge is a word‑processor feature that combines a main document (the template) with a data source (a list of variable information such as names, addresses, or roll numbers) to produce a set of merged documents — one personalized copy for each record in the data source. The process involves three core sub‑concepts: 1. Main Document – contains the fixed text and placeholders called merge fields (e.g., «First_Name», «City»). 2. Data Source – a structured table (often a spreadsheet, CSV file, or an address book) where each row represents one recipient and each column matches a merge field. 3. Merge Operation – the engine that reads each row, substitutes the fields in the main document, and outputs a new document or prints directly. The Mail Merge Wizard (or step‑by‑step pane) guides the user through: selecting the document type (letters, envelopes, labels, email), choosing the starting document, connecting to the data source, inserting merge fields, previewing results, and completing the merge. Understanding the relationship between the template and the data source is essential; the template never changes, while the data source supplies the variable parts. This node focuses on the procedural workflow — the exact clicks and decisions a Class 6 student must make to run a successful mail merge in a typical ICSE‑approved word processor (e.g., LibreOffice Writer or MS Word).
steps: The Mail Merge Wizard turns a single template into many personalized documents by stepping through six fixed stages.
Here is why: each stage isolates one decision so the user cannot skip a required link between template and data.
Consider a Class 6 project where you must send “Library Overdue Notice” letters to 15 students. 1.
Choose Document Type – Open the wizard (Tools → Mail Merge Wizard).
Select “Letters” because each notice is a full‑page letter. 2.
Select Starting Document – Pick “Use the current document” if you already typed the notice; otherwise choose “Start from a template” and pick a blank letter layout. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Select recipients first”) reveals the misconception that data source selection precedes document type, confusing the logical order where the output format determines later choices.
remember: What is the first step in the Mail Merge Wizard.
Why must the column headers in the data source exactly match the merge field names you insert.
During preview you notice that «DueDate» appears as «DueDate» instead of a date. Evaluate the likely cause.

cards.title: Preparing the main document is the construction of the merge's fixed component…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Preparing the main document is the construction of the merge's fixed component: the complete letter, notice, certificate or label design — every shared word, line and layout finished to print quality — with merge fields inserted at the exact positions where each copy's changing values must appear. A merge field is inserted with the word processor's own merge-field command while the data source is attached; it appears in the document as a marked slot (for example «Student_Name») and is stored as a LINK to a named column of the list, never as typed text. Three placement rules govern the slots. Rule of consumption: a slot exists only where the sentence genuinely consumes a changing fact — the greeting, the addressed detail, the quoted value; fixed facts (the school's name, the date if common) are typed as ordinary text. Rule of the exact name: a slot's field name must match its column's name in the data source letter for letter — «Name» cannot read a column called "Student_Name" — because the bridge between letter and list is the name itself. Rule of the reading test: after inserting, the builder reads each sentence with a sample record's values in mind ("Dear Aarav, your house Neem...") to confirm the sentence flows as natural prose with real values in place — a slot that makes the sentence stumble is misplaced, misnamed or unneeded. The finished main document is one design saved as a file: it is attached to the data source at merge time, and because slots live in it by name, the same document can serve an improved list without editing, and the same list can serve many documents without retyping.
steps: The takeaway first: the main document is written once to full print quality with the changing positions left to merge fields — inserted by the field command, named exactly as the list's columns, and verified by reading…
Supporting arguments: 1.

The letter is finished BEFORE the slots go in. A main document is not a template of empty gaps — it is the complete letter, typed, formatted, proofread, with the merge fields dropped into an already-flowing text.
Writing the prose around real placeholder positions (not blank underlines) means the merged copies inherit a polished letter, not a form with holes. 2.
Slots are placed by consumption, and consumption is rare.
Read the draft sentence by sentence and ask one question: does this exact position change per recipient?
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "place a slot wherever the page looks empty so the list gets used") reveals use-the-list thinking — the list serves the letter, never the reverse; an unconsumed column simply stays unread, and an invented slot manufactures a defect.
remember: Recall: State the three placement rules for merge fields, each with its one-line meaning.
Reasoning: A student argues: "I typed «Name» directly into the letter — it looks exactly the same as the inserted field, so it will merge the same way." Explain what actually….
Evaluate: A main document for the annual report circular contains 22 merge fields, including «School_Name», «Academic_Year», «Term», «Principal_Name» and «Reporting_Date» — all….

cards.title: Running the merge is the execution stage of mail merge…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Running the merge is the execution stage of mail merge: with the main document and data source complete and attached, the builder previews the merged copies (stepping through the records on screen, the document showing itself filled with each record's values in turn), then merges to output — either to a new document (one file containing all the finished copies, separated page by page, which can be saved, proofread and printed at will) or directly to the printer (copies stream to paper without an intermediate file). After the run, the count check confirms the copies produced equal the records merged, and the merged output — or the print job — is verified against a sample before distribution. The stage is governed by a fixed order: attach → preview → merge → verify. Attaching links the list to the document (if not already linked during field insertion,). Previewing is deliberately placed before any output exists: it is the last stage where every defect — an empty slot from an incomplete record, a literal field from typed text, a mis-placed slot — costs one edit instead of one reprint batch. Merging to a new document is the default professional choice because it makes the output inspectable and re-printable; merging directly to the printer is the fast path reserved for lists already proven by a previous preview. Verify closes the stage: count the copies against the records, read one front, one middle, one back copy against its record — the batch is finished when it has been counted and sampled, not merely produced.
steps: The takeaway first: the merge runs in one disciplined sequence — attach, preview every record, merge to a new document by default, then verify by count and by sample — and the sequence exists because the preview is the…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Attach first, because fields resolve against an attached list.
The merge fields in the letter are links to column NAMES; attaching the data source is what lets the engine offer those names and later find each record's values.
A merge attempted without a live attachment resolves nothing — the machine runs out of empty slots before it runs out of records. 2.
Preview is the reading test grown to full size.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., putting merge before preview "because the computer is faster at it") reveals output-first impatience — the run is deterministic and will faithfully stamp whatever exists, including defects; the order's whole point is that inspection…
remember: Recall: List the four steps of running a merge in order, and state the purpose of each in one line.
Reasoning: A classmate asks: "Why merge to a new document at….
Evaluate: An office runner proposes: "Preview just the first copy — if it is right, the rest are right, because the letter is the same." Evaluate on three grounds: what the first….

cards.title: Previewing merged documents is the step in a mail merge where the word…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Previewing merged documents is the step in a mail merge where the word processor displays each personalized copy of the main document after merging it with the data source. The main document contains static text and merge fields (placeholders like «FirstName», «Address»). The data source holds rows of variable information (names, addresses). When the merge is executed, the processor generates a temporary merged document for every record. The preview pane lets the user navigate record by record, inspect the result, and edit individual letters without altering the main template or the data source. This step ensures accuracy — catching missing fields, formatting glitches, or data entry errors — before committing to print or saving the output as a single file or separate files. It connects the earlier stages (creating the main document, linking the data source, inserting merge fields) to the final output stage (printing, emailing, or saving). The preview also offers options to exclude specific recipients, print a range of records, or save the merged set as a new document for later editing.
steps: Previewing merged documents is the safety net that catches mistakes before they reach paper.
Here is why: the main document and data source may look correct separately, but combined they can produce misaligned addresses, missing punctuation, or wrong field order.
First, after inserting all merge fields, click the “Preview Results” button on the Mailings tab; the first merged letter appears with real data from the first record.
Second, use the Next and Previous record arrows to scroll through each cousin’s invitation, checking that «FirstName» «LastName» appears correctly and that the address lines wrap neatly.

Third, if you spot a typo — say “Mumbi” instead of “Mumbai” — click inside the preview, edit the text, and the change applies only to that merged copy; the main template and data source stay untouched.

Fourth, when satisfied, choose “Finish & Merge” → “Print Documents” to send all letters to the printer, or “Edit Individual Documents” to save the whole set as a new file where each letter is a separate section.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Finish & Merge”) reveals the misconception that preview and final output are the same step — confusing the checking phase with the production phase.
remember: What button on the Mailings tab starts the preview of merged documents.
Why does editing text in the preview pane not change the main document or the data source.
A student previews 15 merged letters and notices that the 7th letter has an extra blank line before the address. Evaluate whether fixing this in the preview is the best approach.

cards.title: Merge troubleshooting is the professional discipline of diagnosing defective…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Merge troubleshooting is the professional discipline of diagnosing defective merged output by mapping each visible defect back to its component of origin — the MAIN DOCUMENT (design defects: slotted fixed facts, mis-slotted positions, typed pseudo-fields, wrong-form field names), the DATA SOURCE (data defects: empty cells, wrong values, inconsistent value formats, duplicate or junk records), or the RUN (procedure defects: ranged merges, stale-list merges, skipped previews) — repairing at the component, and re-running with the affected range re-previewed. The discipline's three rules: diagnose before touching (read the defect's signature: uniform-across-batch points to the document; scattered-by-record points to the list; count-mismatch points to the run), repair at the source (edit the list cell or the letter field — never the printed or merged copy, which is output and will be regenerated), and re-verify the scope (a local fix re-previews its neighbourhood; a global fix re-previews everything). The node also collects the working rules that prevent the catalogue: preview is non-negotiable and full (every record); the count check runs on every merge; fields are inserted only by command (never typed); lists are complete and plain before running ('s four rules); edits between preview and merge invalidate the preview for the changed range; and every run is closed by count-plus-sample before anything is distributed. With these, the merge's failure modes become a finite, nameable list — each with a signature, a cause, a repair, and a prevention.
steps: The takeaway first: every merge defect belongs to exactly one of three components — document, list, or run — its signature tells you which before you touch anything, the only honest repair is at the component itself…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Signatures come first because they are free.

Uniform defect (every copy wrong the same way) = DOCUMENT — the mould is flawed, so every casting shows it. Scattered defect (some copies, different ways) = LIST — some records are incomplete or wrong.
Count mismatch = RUN — the merge walked a different population than intended.
Reading the signature takes ten seconds and prevents the classic repair error: re-typing the letter when one cell was empty. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., classifying the literal «Name» as a list defect "because names come from the list") reveals component-blindness — the list's names are fine; the LETTER never asked for them, because the slot was typed…
remember: Recall: Name the three components a merge defect can belong to, the output signature of each, and one example defect per component.
Reasoning: The rule says "repair at the source — never the output." A clerk objects: "The merged file is on the computer — editing IT is also electronic, so it is a source.….
Evaluate: After a defective batch, the clerk's report reads: "Defect: three letters had blank….

cards.title: Mail-merge synthesis is the execution of the complete chapter method…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Mail-merge synthesis is the execution of the complete chapter method — design the list, write the letter, link the fields, run with preview, verify by count and sample, extend to envelopes and labels, and diagnose by signature — as ONE working sequence on real documents. It is not a new feature: it is the chapter's seven skills in their working order, with the discipline that binds them (complete plain lists; command-inserted fields; full previews before output; count gates and register samples; repair-at-source; scoped re-verification). The method, restated as one chain: (1) SURVEY — read the planned outputs, harvest the union of their field needs, refuse dead-weight fields; (2) BUILD THE LIST — first row = unique field names, one complete record per recipient, every cell filled, strictly rectangular; (3) WRITE THE LETTER — fixed prose finished to print quality, slots inserted by command with names chosen from the list; (4) RUN — attach, preview EVERY record, merge to a new document; (5) VERIFY — count (copies = records) plus first/middle/last samples against the register, plus the layout checks for envelope/label outputs; (6) MAINTAIN — corrections at the source (list cell or letter field), scoped re-previews, issues archived by date. Synthesis also means knowing the COST MAP: every defect is cheapest at its home checkpoint and dearer at each later one — a missing cell costs a keystroke at the list pass, a re-preview at the run, and an apology after the post.
steps: The takeaway first: the chapter is one method, not seven topics — survey, list, letter, run, verify, maintain — and exam marks come from running the chain in order, from knowing which checkpoint owns each task, and from…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Checkpoint order is cost order.
A missing cell costs one keystroke at the list pass; the same cell costs a re-preview if found at the run, and an apology letter if found by the recipient.
Every checkpoint freezes what the next depends on — the list names feed the letter's slots; the previewed state feeds the merge; the verified batch feeds the post.
The chain runs one way because repair costs run one way. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing the letter before the list) reveals order-blindness — the letter's slots are chosen FROM the list's names; building the mould before knowing the material's shape is the chapter's most expensive reversal.
remember: Recall: List the six links of the mail-merge chain in order and name one defining action of each.
Reasoning: A submitted merge project shows: a letter whose greeting reads "Dear «Name»" on all copies; three copies with blank house slots; and a merged file holding 38 copies for….
Evaluate: A classmate announces his workflow: "I skip the list passes and preview instead — the preview shows everything the passes would find, so one walk saves two stages.….

cards.title: The chapter “Presentation” introduces the core building blocks of a digital…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: The chapter “Presentation” introduces the core building blocks of a digital slideshow used in Class 6 Computer Studies under the CISCE ICSE curriculum. It covers three interconnected sub‑concepts: 1. Slides – the individual pages that hold text, images, shapes, and multimedia. A slide is the canvas where content is arranged using layouts, placeholders, and formatting tools. 2. Transitions – the visual effects that control how one slide replaces the previous one during a slide show (e.g., fade, push, wipe). Transitions apply to the whole slide and determine the flow between slides. 3. Animations – the motion effects applied to individual objects (text boxes, pictures, charts) within a slide. Animations control entrance, emphasis, exit, and motion paths, allowing objects to appear, move, or disappear in a sequenced manner. These three layers work together: slides provide structure, transitions give the show a rhythm, and animations add detail and emphasis. Mastery of all three enables a student to create clear, engaging, and well‑timed presentations for class projects, assemblies, or competitions.
steps: A good presentation is built from three layers — slides give structure, transitions give flow, and animations give emphasis.
Here is why: each layer solves a different communication problem.
Slides organise information into digestible chunks, like pages in a notebook.
Transitions act like the turning of pages, preventing abrupt jumps that distract the audience.
Animations highlight key points inside a page, guiding the viewer’s eye to the most important data.
Consider a Class 6 science project on “Water Cycle”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “slides, themes, and templates”) reveals the misconception that design themes are a separate visual‑effect layer, confusing formatting with motion effects.
remember: What are the three main visual‑effect categories covered in this chapter.
Why does a presentation need both transitions and animations instead of just one of them.
Evaluate the statement: “Adding many different transition effects makes a presentation more professional.”.

cards.title: Visual effects in a presentation are the graphical techniques that control how…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Visual effects in a presentation are the graphical techniques that control how slides appear, change, and how objects on a slide behave. A slide is the basic canvas that holds text, images, charts, and multimedia. Transitions are effects applied between two consecutive slides; they determine the visual change when the presentation moves from one slide to the next (e.g., fade, push, wipe, cover). Animations are effects applied to individual objects (text boxes, pictures, shapes) within a single slide; they define entrance, emphasis, exit, and motion‑path behaviours (e.g., appear, fly‑in, pulse, spin). The three concepts are hierarchical: a presentation consists of ordered slides; each slide may have a transition governing its entry; each object on a slide may have one or more animations governing its behaviour. Proper use improves clarity, guides audience attention, and reinforces the narrative flow, while overuse can distract or confuse.
steps: Visual effects turn a static stack of slides into a guided story.
The one thing to remember: transitions control the hand‑over between slides, while animations control the life of objects inside a slide.
Here is why: a presentation is a sequence; the audience needs a clear signal when a new idea begins — that is the transition.
Inside each idea, the speaker may want to reveal points one by one — that is animation.
Consider a Class 6 project on “Festivals of India”.
Slide 1 shows the title; a Fade transition gently brings Slide 2 (Diwali) into view.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “both are the same thing”) reveals the misconception that any visual effect is interchangeable, ignoring the hierarchical scope of transitions versus animations.
remember: What is the main difference between a slide transition and an object animation.
If a teacher wants the title of a slide to appear first, then each bullet point to appear one after another on click, which effects should be applied and to what.
Evaluate the statement: “Using many different transitions in one presentation makes it more professional.”.

cards.title: A transition in presentation software is a visual effect applied to the change…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A transition in presentation software is a visual effect applied to the change between two consecutive slides. It controls how the outgoing slide leaves the screen and how the incoming slide appears. Transitions can be simple (cut, fade) or dynamic (push, wipe, cover, uncover, morph). Each transition has properties such as duration (speed), direction (from left, right, top, bottom), and sound (optional audio cue). Transitions are applied to the slide level, not to individual objects; they affect the whole slide canvas. They differ from animations, which act on elements inside a slide. Proper use of transitions guides audience attention, signals topic changes, and maintains flow without distracting from content. Overuse or overly flashy transitions can reduce readability and professionalism. In CISCE ICSE Class 6 Computer Studies, students learn to select, customize, and preview transitions using the software’s Transitions tab, and to apply them consistently across a presentation.
steps: A transition is the bridge that carries the audience from one slide to the next, and choosing the right bridge keeps the story smooth.
Here is why: transitions signal a change of idea, they set the pace, and they can reinforce the mood of the presentation.

Consider a school project on Indian festivals: you might use a gentle Fade between slides describing Diwali and Holi to show a calm flow, but a Push from left when moving from a history slide to a quiz slide to add…
First, open the Transitions tab in your presentation software.
Second, click the slide thumbnail you want to leave.
Third, browse the gallery — Subtle (Cut, Fade, Push), Exciting (Wheel, Zoom, Flip), Dynamic (Morph, Pan).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “transitions animate individual objects on a slide”) reveals the misconception that transitions and animations are the same — confusing slide‑level effects with object‑level effects.
remember: What is the primary purpose of a slide transition in a presentation.
If a student sets a transition duration to 0.5 seconds and another to 5 seconds, how will the audience experience differ.
Evaluate the statement: “Using a different exciting transition on every slide makes a presentation more engaging.”.

cards.title: An animation is a visual effect applied to an individual OBJECT on a slide…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: An animation is a visual effect applied to an individual OBJECT on a slide — a title, a bullet point, a picture, a shape, a table — controlling how that object appears, draws attention, or leaves. The four animation types: entrance effects (how an object arrives — Appear, Fade In, Fly In from a side), emphasis effects (an object already visible draws the eye — Grow/Shrink, Change Colour, Pulse), exit effects (how an object leaves — Fade Out, Fly Out), and motion paths (the object travels along a drawn route across the slide). Each animation carries settings: the start condition — on click (the object waits for the speaker's click; the professional default), with previous (arrives together with the last effect), or after previous (arrives automatically once the last effect finishes); plus duration (how long the effect takes) and delay (wait before it begins). Objects on one slide animate in a numbered sequence, listed in the animation pane, where effects can be reordered. This node is layer three of Topic 5's three-layer system: animations move objects INSIDE a slide — the slides were built in and the page-to-page movement set in. The node's working skill is the click-by-click reveal: a slide's bullet points are given entrance effects set to "on click", so the audience hears each point as the speaker speaks it and reads it the moment it is discussed — the speaker, not the slide, controls the pace of the page. The governing rules: animations exist to direct attention, never to decorate — an entrance timed to the talk is a servant; a spinning heading is a rival. And less is more: one or two animated reveals on the slides that need them beat animated everything on every slide.
steps: The takeaway first: an animation is a spotlight you schedule — it makes one object on a slide arrive, stand out or leave at a moment the speaker chooses, and its professional use is the click-by-click reveal: points…
Supporting arguments: 1.
The four types answer four different questions.
Entrance answers "how does it arrive?" (Appear — instantly there;
Fade In — gently there;
Fly In — there from a direction).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calling the fade between slides an animation, or Appear a transition) reveals layer-blur — the same motion word can name either layer, and the exam's distinction is always WHAT moves: the page (transition) or an object on it (animation).
remember: Recall: Define an animation, state what it applies to, and name the four animation types with one example each.
Reasoning: A speaker's slide shows five bullet points set to appear automatically ("after previous", half-second….
Evaluate: For the "Save Water" show's key slide ("Our Saving Habits" — four points), Riya animates all four points AND the heading AND the water-drop picture — each with a….

cards.title: Running the slideshow is the live delivery skill…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Running the slideshow is the live delivery skill: presenting the finished presentation on the full screen and controlling it in real time. The core operations: start the show (from the beginning, or from the current slide for a mid-deck restart), the full-screen show view (menus vanish; the slide fills the screen), advance to the next slide or the next click-reveal with a click, the spacebar, or a presentation remote, go back one slide for a recap question, the screen-black toggle (the audience's screen goes dark so all eyes return to the speaker during a discussion or while the next activity is set up), jump to a slide by number (typing the number and pressing Enter — for "please show slide 6 again"), and end the show cleanly (the blank closing state or the exit command, not a scramble back into the editor in front of the audience). Alongside the live controls stands the rehearsal habit: running the show end-to-end with a stopwatch and per-slide times, so the group knows its real length (a "ten-minute" show is whatever the stopwatch says), trims content to the available slot, and discovers every misfire — a dead click, a stray effect, a slide in the wrong order — while it is still free to fix. This node is the fourth skill of Topic 5: the slides were built, the transitions dressed, the animations set — this node makes the finished file PERFORM, and feeds its timings and faults back for the design pass and the full workflow synthesis. The governing rule: the show is run, not watched — the presenter owns the pace (click-advance keeps the slides waiting for the talk), and the stopwatch owns the truth (rehearsed timing beats estimated timing, every time).
steps: The takeaway first: a finished file is not a finished show — delivery is its own skill with its own controls: the presenter starts the show, advances in step with the speech, blacks the screen when eyes must return…
The show view is a different room.
The editor shows one slide surrounded by panels; the show view is full-screen, menu-less, and irreversible-feeling to beginners.

The five controls end the fear: start (from beginning for the real show, from current slide when fixing one), advance (click/spacebar/remote), back (for the recap question that always comes), jump-to-number (type the…
Ten minutes of deliberate practice makes the live room as familiar as the editor. 2.
Click-advance makes the speaker the clock.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing "save" or "print" among the live controls, or using exit-to-editor as the ending) reveals editor-thinking — the show view has its own small control set, and a professional close is the end command, not a visible dive back into…
remember: Recall: Name the live slideshow controls a presenter uses, and state the moment each is used.
Reasoning: A group's show is allotted five minutes but its first timed rehearsal reads 7 minutes….
Evaluate: Two presenters handle the same interruption: mid-show, the teacher says, "Stop — let us discuss the map for two minutes, then continue." Presenter A keeps the map slide….

cards.title: Slide design discipline is the set of rules that makes a slideshow readable…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Slide design discipline is the set of rules that makes a slideshow readable from the back row and easy to listen to. The rules cluster into four groups. Text rules: large fonts (headings roughly 36-44 point, body text never below 24 point on a class projector), few points per slide (about six at most), few words per point (about six), sentence-case text rather than full paragraphs. Contrast rules: dark text on a light background or light text on a dark one — strong, plain contrast; never similar tones, never busy photographs behind text; consistent colours drawn from a small palette. Consistency rules: one or two fonts for the whole show (one for headings, optionally one for body), the same point style on every slide, the same heading position — set once via the slide master/layout rather than re-decided per slide. Effect-budget rules: the show carries ONE transition style throughout and animations only where a reveal serves the talk; every effect must pass the attention test — it directs the audience to content at the moment the content matters — or it is refused. This node is the design pass of Topic 5: the mechanical skills are all in place (slides, transitions, animations, delivery); this node supplies the JUDGMENT layer — the checklist a group runs over its finished show to find what a first-time audience would suffer: unreadable text, competing colours, decorative motion, and font drift. The governing rule: design is measured at the last bench and by the ear — if the back row cannot read it, the slide failed its one job; if the audience watches the screen instead of the speaker, the effects failed theirs.
steps: The takeaway first: design is the audit layer — four rule clusters (text, contrast, consistency, effect budget) turned into a checklist that a finished show must pass at the last bench and in the ear, and a fix pass…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Numbers make design teachable.
"Make it look nice" is not a rule;

"headings 36-44 point, body at least 24 point, six points of six words, two fonts, one palette, one transition" is. The numbers exist because slides are read from the back: a 24-point line is roughly readable at ten…
Students who memorise the numbers can audit; students who also know the REASONS can defend the numbers in an exam answer. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving four rules all about colours, or citing "make it attractive" as a rule) reveals taste-thinking — the clusters are text, contrast, consistency and…
remember: Recall: State the four design rule clusters and two specific rules from each.
Reasoning: A slide carries eight bullet points in 20-point light-yellow text over a photograph of a river, set in three different….
Evaluate: Two design passes over the same eight-slide….

cards.title: The presentation workflow is the ordered production sequence that turns a topic…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: The presentation workflow is the ordered production sequence that turns a topic into a delivered show: (1) PLAN — decide the talk's main ideas, one per slide, the slide budget from the time slot (roughly 40-45 seconds per slide), and the style sheet (fonts, palette, transition, animation policy) before any software is opened; (2) BUILD — create the slides in the chosen layouts, fill placeholders, seat pictures, write speaker notes ('s skills); (3) DRESS — apply the one transition show-wide and the budgeted click-reveals (05_003 and 05_004's skills); (4) REHEARSE — timed full runs with a fault log, then the trim arithmetic, then the design audit and the two acceptance tests (05_005 and 05_006's skills); (5) PRESENT — the live show under control discipline; and (6) REVIEW — the post-show log: what over-ran, which questions came, what the next show inherits. Each stage's output is the next stage's input: the plan's slide list builds the deck, the built deck takes the dressing, the dressed show is rehearsed into a measured show, the measured show is presented, and the presented show feeds the review that improves the next plan. This node is the assembly node of Topic 5: every individual skill now exists (slides 05_002, transitions 05_003, animations 05_004, delivery 05_005, design 05_006); the workflow teaches their ORDER and their HANDSHAKES — what each stage must hand the next so nothing is discovered late. Its artefact is the plan sheet: one document holding the slide list, budgets, style sheet, fault log and review notes — the show's paper twin that makes the process visible, divisible among group members, and examinable. The governing rule: each stage exists to catch its own class of mistake — planning catches wrong content, rehearsal catches wrong timing, the audit catches wrong style; a stage skipped is not time saved but its mistakes deferred to the most expensive place: the stage in front of an audience.
steps: The takeaway first: the workflow is the chapter as an assembly line — plan, build, dress, rehearse, present, review — where each stage catches its own class of mistake and hands a verified artefact to the next, so that…
Planning first is the cheapest stage and the strongest.

Fifteen minutes with paper — slide list, budgets, style sheet, roles — decides the show's shape before a single click; every change made on paper costs an eraser, the same change made after building costs slides, and…
The plan sheet is also how a group divides work without collision: build, pictures, notes, stack-keeping are assignable regions only when the slide list exists to assign against. 2.
The handshakes are where quality is actually enforced.
Build hands Dress a placeholder-pure stack (or the show-wide restyle will not land);
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., dressing before building is complete, or placing the design audit before rehearsal) reveals order-blindness — each stage consumes the previous stage's verified output; rehearsal audits the DRESSED show because timing depends on the…
remember: Recall: Name the six workflow stages in order and state what each contributes.
Reasoning: A group completes BUILD in one period and jumps straight to PRESENT, skipping DRESS and REHEARSE because "the slides are all there — how hard can the rest be?" Predict….
Evaluate: Two four-member groups produce shows for the same….

cards.title: This node synthesises the three visual‑effect concepts introduced earlier…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: This node synthesises the three visual‑effect concepts introduced earlier — slides, transitions, and animations — into a coherent framework for creating effective presentations and for answering CISCE‑style examination questions. A slide is the static canvas that holds text, images, and shapes. A transition governs how one slide replaces the previous one (e.g., fade, push, wipe) and sets the pacing of the whole show. An animation controls the entrance, emphasis, or exit of individual objects on a slide (e.g., appear, pulse, motion path). The synthesis emphasises that transitions affect the narrative flow between slides, while animations direct attention within a slide; both must be chosen to support the message, not merely to decorate. Exam patterns in CISCE Class 6 Computer Studies typically ask students to (a) identify the correct transition or animation for a given scenario, (b) predict the visual outcome of a sequence of effects, (c) spot inappropriate or excessive use of effects, and (d) justify design choices in short‑answer questions. Mastery requires linking the purpose of each effect to audience comprehension, recognising common presets in presentation software, and applying design principles such as consistency, restraint, and relevance.
steps: A good presentation uses slide transitions and object animations purposefully to guide the audience’s attention without distracting them.

First, transitions set the rhythm of the whole story; a consistent “fade” across all slides feels like turning pages of a book, while a “push” can suggest forward movement, useful for a timeline of Indian freedom…
Second, animations highlight key points on each slide; a “wipe” entrance for a bullet list reveals ideas one by one, letting the class absorb each fact before the next appears.

Third, overusing flashy effects such as “spin” or “bounce” creates visual noise, making it harder for viewers to focus on the content — just as too many fireworks obscure the night sky. Fourth, the order of animations…
Fifth, previewing the show in “Slide Show” mode lets the creator verify timing and flow, ensuring that the effects serve the narrative.
Consider a Class 6 project on “States of India”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to make text move on the slide”) reveals the misconception that transitions affect object‑level movement rather than slide‑level change.
remember: What is the primary purpose of a slide transition in a presentation.
If a student applies a “spin” animation to every bullet point on a slide, what is the likely impact on audience comprehension.
Evaluate the suitability of using a “push” transition for a presentation that compares two similar products side by side on consecutive slides.

cards.title: Scratch is a visual, block-based programming language and environment in which…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Scratch is a visual, block-based programming language and environment in which programs — called projects — are built by snapping together colour-coded blocks instead of typing text. Its cast: the stage, the 480x360 rectangle where everything is seen; sprites, the characters and objects (the cat mascot, a basket, a falling mango) that act on the stage; costumes, the different looks a sprite can wear; backdrops, the stage's backgrounds; and scripts, the stacked sequences of blocks that give a sprite its behaviour. The blocks live in a palette organised into categories by colour — Motion (blue: move, turn, glide, change x/y), Looks (purple: say, switch costume, change size), Sound (pink: play sounds), Events (yellow: when green flag clicked, when key pressed), Control (orange: forever, repeat, if...then, if...else, wait), Sensing (light blue: touching?, key pressed?, mouse position), Operators (green: pick random, arithmetic, comparisons) and Variables (orange: score, lives, make a variable). This chapter, Topic 6: Scratch Programming — Introduction to Game Creation, teaches programming through building a game, because a game forces every core idea into play at once: a game is a loop that never stops until the game ends, events that respond to the player's keys, conditions that decide win and lose, sensing that detects the catch, and variables that remember the score. The chapter's central idea: a program is behaviour you design — the sprite does exactly what your blocks say, nothing more and nothing less, and that exactness is both the joy (the character truly obeys you) and the lesson (the computer never guesses). The chapter travels through six working skills, one per concept node: understanding the game-creation idea and the Scratch environment (sprites, stage, scripts); motion and looks — moving sprites, coordinates, and showing what is happening; events and control — key presses, forever loops, and if decisions; sensing and scoring — detecting touches and keeping score with variables; building and debugging a complete catch-the-mangoes game; and game design with polish — planning, sound, levels, and sharing. The final node gathers the topic for exams.
steps: The takeaway first: Scratch turns programming into building with blocks — sprites are the actors, the stage is their world, scripts are their behaviour, and a game is the perfect first program because it forces the five…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Blocks remove the wall between idea and program.

In typed languages a missing comma breaks everything and the beginner never finds it; in Scratch a block only snaps where it fits — a motion block cannot attach to the wrong kind of slot — so whole classes of typing…
The beginner's full attention goes to the real question of programming: WHAT should happen, and in WHAT order? 2.
The sprite-stage model is small enough to hold in the head.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a sprite is a picture and a costume is a character") reveals role-swap — the sprite is the actor (it can move and carry scripts), the costume is only one of its looks; the exam awards marks for each part's exact job.
remember: Recall: Define Scratch and name the parts of its environment — stage, sprite, costume, backdrop, script — with one line on each.
Reasoning: A classmate says, "Scratch is not real programming because you do not type code." Using the five big ideas this chapter builds through games, argue what Scratch….
Evaluate: Two students plan their first Scratch….

cards.title: Game creation in Scratch is the process of designing an interactive experience…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Game creation in Scratch is the process of designing an interactive experience by assembling visual programming blocks that control sprites — graphical actors — on a stage. Each sprite owns a set of scripts, which are sequences of blocks triggered by events such as the green flag, key presses, or messages received from other sprites. Core concepts include: sprites (characters with costumes and sounds), stage (background and coordinate system), events (entry points for scripts), control structures (forever loops, repeat loops, conditionals) that dictate flow, variables (named storage for data like score or lives), sensing blocks (detecting touch, colour, distance), and broadcasting (sending messages to coordinate multiple sprites). A game typically defines an objective (e.g., reach a score), rules (collision detection, boundaries), feedback (sound, visual changes), and a win/lose condition. The relationship among these elements is hierarchical: events start scripts, control structures orchestrate repeated or conditional actions, sensing provides input for decisions, variables hold state, and broadcasting synchronises independent sprites. Mastery of these building blocks enables a learner to translate a game idea into a functioning Scratch project.
steps: A game in Scratch is built by giving each sprite a set of instructions that respond to events, repeat actions, make decisions, and share information through variables and messages.

Here is why: first, sprites are the actors that carry out every visible action; second, events such as the green flag or a key press decide when a script starts; third, loops like forever keep the game running…
Consider the classic playground game “Chor Police” where one child chases others.
In Scratch we can model this as a “Cat and Mouse” game.
Step 1: Open Scratch and delete the default cat. Choose a cat sprite for the chaser and a mouse sprite for the runner.
Step 2: Add a backdrop of a park.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "Control") reveals the misconception that any block that starts a script belongs to Control, confusing event triggers with flow‑control structures like loops and conditionals.
remember: What block category in Scratch contains the "when green flag clicked" block.
If a sprite has a "forever" loop containing "move 10 steps" and "if on edge, bounce", what will happen when the green flag is clicked.
A student uses a "repeat 10" loop to increase the score each time the cat touches the mouse. Is this correct? Why or why not.

cards.title: In Scratch, a sprite is an independent graphical object that can move, speak…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: In Scratch, a sprite is an independent graphical object that can move, speak, and interact with other sprites on the stage. Every sprite owns a collection of costumes; each costume is a single image that represents one visual state of the sprite. By rapidly switching between costumes, a sprite appears to animate — for example, a bird flapping its wings uses two or more costumes showing wings up and wings down. The stage itself has backdrops, which are full‑screen images that set the scene for the whole project. Only one backdrop is visible at a time, but a project can contain many backdrops and switch among them to show different levels, menus, or story settings. Sprites and the stage operate in parallel: a sprite’s costume changes do not affect the backdrop, and a backdrop change does not alter a sprite’s current costume. The relationship is hierarchical — the stage holds backdrops, each sprite holds its own costumes, and scripts attached to a sprite or the stage control when switches happen using blocks such as `next costume`, `switch costume to`, `switch backdrop to`, and `next backdrop`. Understanding this separation is essential because game logic often depends on coordinating sprite animation (costume changes) with scene transitions (backdrop changes).
steps: In Scratch, every game character is a sprite that changes its appearance through costumes, while the stage changes its scenery through backdrops.
First, sprites act as independent actors — each one carries its own scripts, sounds, and costumes, so a cat sprite and a dog sprite can animate simultaneously without interfering.
Second, costumes are the frames of animation — just as a flipbook shows motion by flipping pages, a sprite shows motion by switching costumes in sequence.
Third, backdrops set the scene — they are like changing the stage curtain between acts; a jungle backdrop can become a city backdrop when the player reaches a new level.
Fourth, the `next costume` block cycles forward through a sprite’s costume list, looping back to the first after the last, which is perfect for continuous animation like walking.
Fifth, the `switch backdrop to` block lets a script decide exactly which backdrop to show, enabling story branches or level changes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “backdrop”) reveals the misconception that the stage’s background images belong to a sprite — confusing stage‑level assets with sprite‑level assets.
remember: What is the term for a single image that represents one visual state of a sprite in Scratch.
If a sprite has three costumes named “walk1”, “walk2”, “walk3” and a script runs `repeat 6 [ next costume ]`, which costume will be shown at the end.
A student claims that changing a sprite’s costume also changes the stage backdrop. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Event and Control are the two block categories that give a Scratch project its…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Event and Control are the two block categories that give a Scratch project its timing and its decision-making. Event blocks (yellow) are hat blocks — rounded on top, flat-bottomed, and unable to have anything snapped above them — whose only job is to START a script when something happens. The category contains when green flag clicked (start on the flag), when [space] key pressed (start on any keyboard key), when this sprite clicked and when stage clicked (start on a mouse click on the sprite or stage), when backdrop switches to [name] (start on a scene change), and when I receive [message] together with the stack blocks broadcast [message] and broadcast [message] and wait (start on a message sent by another script). Several event hats can coexist in one project, each starting its own script independently. Control blocks (orange) are stack and C-shaped blocks that shape what happens AFTER a script starts: wait [n] seconds pauses the script; repeat [n] runs the blocks inside it a fixed number of times; forever runs them endlessly; if...then runs the blocks inside only when a hexagonal condition is true; if...then...else chooses between two block groups; wait until and repeat until pause or loop until a condition becomes true; and stop [all / this script / other scripts in sprite] halts chosen scripts. In short: events decide WHEN a script wakes up, control decides HOW MANY times, HOW LONG, and WHETHER each piece of it runs — the difference between a starting gun and the rules of the race.
steps: The takeaway first: every Scratch script answers three questions — WHEN does it start (an event hat), HOW MANY times does it act (a loop), and WHETHER a piece runs at all (a condition) — and mastering the Event and…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Hat blocks are the only doors into a program.
No matter how beautiful a stack of blocks is, it is dead until an event hat wakes it. That is why the very first debugging question in any project is: "which hat is this stack wearing?"
Loops give scripts their lifetime.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "Motion starts the script because the sprite moves first") reveals the misconception that the first visible action block is the cause of running — the motion block only acts AFTER an event hat has started the script; without a hat the…

cards.title: A variable in Scratch is a named storage container that holds a value…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: A variable in Scratch is a named storage container that holds a value — either a number or a piece of text — which can be read and changed while a project runs. When you click Make a Variable in the Variables palette, you give it a name (for example, Score) and choose its scope: for all sprites (global) or for this sprite only (local). A global variable can be read and modified by any sprite and the stage; a local variable is private to the sprite that owns it. Once created, Scratch automatically provides blocks to set the variable to a specific value, change it by an amount, show or hide its monitor on the stage, and to use its current value inside other blocks (such as inside an if condition or a say block). Variables interact closely with control structures introduced earlier: a forever loop can repeatedly change a variable, an if block can test a variable’s value to decide what happens next, and broadcast messages can trigger scripts that read or write variables. Understanding variable scope, initialisation (usually done when the green flag is clicked), and the difference between set (assign) and change (increment/decrement) is essential for building games that keep score, count lives, track time, or manage levels.
steps: Variables in Scratch act like labelled boxes that store numbers or text, letting a game remember and change information such as the player’s score.
First, a variable must be created from the Variables palette; choosing for all sprites makes the box visible to every sprite, while for this sprite only keeps it private.
Second, the variable needs an initial value — usually set to 0 when the green flag is clicked — so the game starts from a known state.
Third, the change block modifies the stored value without erasing the previous content, which is perfect for adding points or subtracting lives.
Fourth, the show variable block puts a monitor on the stage so players can see the current value in real time.
Fifth, conditional blocks (if) can read the variable to trigger events, such as ending the game when Lives reaches 0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the set block creates a variable") reveals the misconception that assignment blocks also declare variables — confusing initialisation with declaration.
remember: What block is used to create a new variable in Scratch.

cards.title: Game assembly is the stage of Scratch programming where previously learnt…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: Game assembly is the stage of Scratch programming where previously learnt pieces — event hats, motion and looks blocks, loops, conditions, sensing and variables — are combined into a multi-script project that behaves as one coherent game. Assembly introduces two structural ideas. Nesting means placing one control structure inside another: a repeat inside a forever, an if inside a repeat, or an if inside an if — the inner structure completes all its passes (or tests) for every single pass of the outer one, so nesting multiplies behaviour. Difficulty progression means using a variable not just as a score but as a control value: when Score crosses a threshold, the game changes a Speed variable or switches a backdrop, so the same blocks produce harder play — levels without new code. Debugging is the systematic discipline of finding and removing faults: reproducing the wrong behaviour, predicting what the script SHOULD do block by block, tracing what it actually does (monitors, say-block probes, single runs), isolating the faulty block or misplaced boundary, fixing one thing at a time, and re-testing until prediction and observation agree. A finished assembled project has the properties CISCE examiners look for: every stack wears a hat, initialisations happen once at the flag, loops contain the blocks that must repeat and nothing else, conditions test the right variable at the right place, and each sprite's role is expressible in one sentence.
steps: The takeaway first: a finished Scratch game is not one big script but several small scripts wearing hats, each answering "who moves, when, how often, and what decides" — and the assembly discipline that gets you there…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Assembly is composition, not invention.

Every block in the finished game is already known; the new skill is the DIVISION OF LABOUR — each sprite gets the minimal scripts that express its one role, and no role is spread across sprites without a broadcast wire.
Initialise once, loop the rest.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "8, because 5 plus 3") reveals the misconception that loops in different levels behave like loops in sequence — addition applies only when the loops are side by side in the script, one after another; nesting is multiplication.
remember: In a nested structure — a repeat 5 placed inside a repeat 3 — how many times do the innermost blocks run in total, and how is the total worked out.

cards.title: The Sound category (magenta/pink) supplies the audio blocks of Scratch…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: The Sound category (magenta/pink) supplies the audio blocks of Scratch, and the Sounds tab of a sprite or the stage supplies the audio files (called sounds, the audio cousins of costumes) that those blocks play. The category contains: start sound [name] — begins playing a sound and immediately continues to the next block (non-blocking); play sound [name] until done — begins playing and HALTS the script until the sound finishes (blocking); stop all sounds — silences every sound in the project at once; change [volume] by [n] and set [volume] to [n] — adjust the loudness of the sprite or stage that owns the script (each sprite and the stage has its own volume, 0–100, default 100). Sounds are attached to sprites (or the stage) through the Sounds tab: choose one from the library, surprise-me, or record your own with the microphone, and edit it with simple tools (louder/softer, faster/slower, fade in/out, reverse). Sound interacts with everything already taught: an event hat (green flag, key press, when I receive) decides WHEN a sound plays; a loop decides HOW OFTEN; start sound inside a busy forever lets effects layer over gameplay, while play sound until done creates a deliberate pause (a jingle must finish before the next scene); and the stage is the natural owner of continuous background music because it has no motion of its own. The one timing rule to respect: a blocking sound inside a loop freezes that loop for the sound's whole duration — which is either exactly the effect you want (a game-over jingle must not be talked over) or a bug (the game stops reacting because the fall loop is sitting inside a 10-second song).
steps: The takeaway first: sound in Scratch is not decoration bolted on at the end — it is behaviour, governed by the same grammar as everything else (an event says WHEN, a loop says HOW OFTEN), with exactly one new idea to…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Sounds belong to sprites, like costumes.
Each sprite — and the stage — has its own Sounds tab, its own volume dial, and its own set of sound names; a block played in the Cat's script uses the Cat's sounds at the Cat's volume.
This ownership is why background music goes on the stage: the stage never moves or changes costume, so a long song attached there never collides with gameplay blocks.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., claiming both blocks play sounds identically and the choice is cosmetic) reveals the misconception that blocking is invisible — the two blocks produce the same audio but different TIMELINES for every block after them, which is a…
remember: Name the Sound block that pauses the script until the sound finishes, and the block that lets the script continue immediately. Give one situation where each is the correct choice.

cards.title: This synthesis node consolidates Topic 6
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition: This synthesis node consolidates Topic 6 (Scratch Programming — Introduction to Game Creation) into one connected competence. The topic's knowledge map has five layers, and examination questions always land on one of them. Layer 1 — the environment: sprites (actors), costumes (looks), backdrops (stage scenes), the block palette's colour-coded categories, the script area, and saving a project. Layer 2 — events: hat blocks (green flag, key press, sprite click, backdrop switch, broadcast/receive) that start scripts — the only doors into execution. Layer 3 — control: loops (repeat, forever, repeat until) that give scripts their lifetime, conditions (if, if...else) that give them judgement, wait that paces them, stop that ends them. Layer 4 — sensing and variables: touching?, key pressed? and kin as the project's perception; variables (set/change, global scope, initialisation at the flag) as its memory — including a variable doubling as a difficulty dial. Layer 5 — assembly craft: one script per job, logic before feedback (sound last in a branch), the two classic traps (multi-fire on touch, stall by blocking sound), and the five-step debugging method (reproduce, predict, trace, isolate, fix-and-retest). CISCE examination of this topic takes recognisable shapes: one-mark definition/name items (blocks, categories, colours), short-answer distinctions (repeat vs forever; start sound vs play sound until done; sprite vs costume), script-writing tasks ("write blocks to…"), output-prediction traces (nested loops, variable changes), and debugging items (find and fix the fault, with the reason). Mastery here means answering ALL five shapes from one mental model.
steps: The takeaway first: Scratch is ONE grammar — an event opens a script, control shapes it, sensing feeds its conditions, variables hold its memory, looks/motion/sound are its output — and a CISCE answer is that same…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Every question names a layer.
"What is a variable?" is Layer 4.
"Distinguish repeat from forever" is Layer 3.
"Write blocks to make the sprite follow the arrow keys" is Layers 2+3+4 composed.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing touching? in Control because it appears inside if blocks) reveals the misconception that location in a script defines category — a sensing block sits inside conditions but belongs to Sensing, exactly as an actor stands on a stage…
remember: To which layer of the Topic 6 map does each block belong — when I receive [message], repeat until, touching [sprite]?, change [Score] by 1, start sound.

cards.title: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language used to create…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language used to create and structure content on the World Wide Web. It uses a system of elements, called tags, to annotate text, images, links, and other media so that a web browser can render them in a meaningful order. The chapter introduces two core ideas: first, the basic tags that mark up headings (`

`–`

`), paragraphs (`

`), line breaks (`
`), images (``), and hyperlinks (``); second, the overall structure of an HTML document, which consists of a root `` element containing a `` section for metadata (title, character set, styles) and a `` section for visible content. Understanding this hierarchy is essential because every webpage follows the same skeleton — doctype declaration, html, head, body — and the tags inside the body define the logical flow of information. The chapter also explains why HTML matters: it is the foundation upon which CSS (styling) and JavaScript (interactivity) are layered, and it enables anyone to publish information globally without proprietary software. By the end of the chapter, students will recognise the purpose of each structural tag, write a minimal valid HTML page, and appreciate how browsers interpret the markup to display a page.
steps: This chapter introduces HTML as the language that structures every webpage, teaching you the essential tags and the overall page skeleton so you can create your own simple web pages.
First, HTML is a markup language, not a programming language; it describes what content is, not how to compute.
Second, every webpage follows a fixed skeleton: a doctype declaration, an `<html>` root, a `<head>` for invisible metadata, and a `<body>` for visible content.
Third, tags come in pairs (opening and closing) and nest like Russian dolls — a paragraph lives inside the body, which lives inside html.
Fourth, the browser reads the markup top‑to‑bottom and builds a visual page accordingly.
Fifth, learning this skeleton lets you publish a page about Diwali celebrations or a cricket scorecard without any special software.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "HTML is a programming language used for calculations") reveals the misconception that markup languages execute logic, confusing HTML with languages like Python or Java.
remember: What does HTML stand for and what is its primary role in a webpage.
Why must every HTML document begin with a doctype declaration.
Evaluate the statement: "The `<head>` section contains everything the user sees on the page.".

cards.title: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language used to create…
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language used to create the structure of web pages. It consists of a set of predefined tags that mark up content so a web browser can render it correctly. The most fundamental tags are the document‑level tags: `` wraps the entire page, `` holds meta‑information like the page title, and `` contains the visible content. Inside ``, heading tags `

` through `

` define hierarchical headings, `

` marks paragraphs, `
` inserts a line break, and `

` draws a thematic horizontal rule. Tags usually come in opening and closing pairs (e.g., `

…

`), and they can be nested to show relationships — a heading inside a section, a paragraph inside a division. This nesting creates a tree‑like structure called the Document Object Model (DOM), which the browser uses to layout the page. Understanding these basic tags is essential because every more complex element (lists, tables, forms, multimedia) builds on the same nesting and pairing principles.
steps: Every webpage is built from a small set of basic HTML tags that define its structure and content.

Here is why: first, tags act like labelled containers — `

` says “this is the most important heading”, `

` says “this is a paragraph”.
Second, tags must be properly nested; a paragraph cannot start inside a heading and end outside it, just as you cannot put a roof on before the walls.
Third, the browser reads the tags in order and builds a tree (the DOM) that determines layout.
Fourth, missing or mismatched tags cause the browser to guess, often producing broken layouts.
Fifth, learning these few tags gives you the power to create any simple page, from a school timetable to a birthday invitation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “`<head>`”) reveals the misconception that the head section contains visible headings, confusing metadata with content structure.

cards.title: The structure of an HTML page is a fixed three-level skeleton.
cards.subject: Computer Studies
cards.definition:
The structure of an HTML page is a fixed three-level skeleton. The entire document is wrapped in the ``... `` container, which declares "everything between us is one HTML page". Inside it live exactly two siblings. The ``... `` section holds information ABOUT the page that is not displayed as page content — its most important member at this level is the ``... `` container, whose text appears in the browser's title bar / on the browser tab, in saved-bookmark lists, and as the name search engines report; it never appears on the page itself. The ``... `` section holds everything the visitor actually sees — headings, paragraphs, breaks and rules from the previous node all live here; exactly one body exists per page. An attribute is extra information written INSIDE an opening tag, always as a `name="value"` pair separated from the tag name by a space: `` colours the page's background yellow and its text navy; `align="center"` on a heading or paragraph (`

`, `

`) places that block; `

` draws a thicker, half-width rule. Attributes belong ONLY in opening tags (never in closing ones), multiple attributes sit side by side separated by spaces, and their values sit inside quotes. Finally, the nesting rule: tags written inside other tags must close in the reverse order of their opening — correct: `

...

`-style layering obeys last-in-first-out, like stacked tiffin boxes; the fault to avoid is OVERLAPPING, e.g., opening A, opening B, closing A, closing B, which tears the structure. The full skeleton — html wrapping head and body, title inside head, content inside body — is the container every later node's tags will be placed into.
steps: The takeaway first: every web page ever written is the same three-box diagram — html wrapping a head (which names the page) and a body (which shows the page) — and the two skills that turn the skeleton into real pages…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Head and body answer different questions.
The head answers "what IS this page?" — its name (title), the kind of text it uses; the body answers "what does the visitor SEE?".
Mixing them up is a visible fault: text written in the head does not appear on the page; a title written in the body appears as ordinary content instead of on the tab.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the title appears as a big heading at the top of the page") reveals the misconception that the title is a visible banner — the page's visible top is a heading tag in the body; the title belongs to the browser's chrome, one level above…
