Here is why: (1) Real‑life situations always involve two linked quantities that change together — like flour and sugar in a recipe, or distance and time at constant speed.
(2) Expressing the link as a ratio makes the relationship explicit and comparable.
(3) A proportion equates two ratios, allowing us to use cross‑multiplication (a·d = b·c) to find a missing value.
(4) The unitary method breaks the problem into “value of one unit” then scales up, which is often more intuitive.
(5) Checking the answer against the story ensures no unit mismatch or logical error.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “cross‑multiply immediately”) reveals the misconception that proportion solving starts with algebra rather than understanding the quantitative relationship.
remember: What is the first step when solving a word problem on ratio and proportion.
A recipe calls for 4 cups of rice for 6 people. How many cups of rice are needed for 9 people? Explain why you set up the proportion as 4/6 = x/9.
A student sets up the proportion 5:8 = 15:x and solves x = 24. Is this correct? Evaluate.

cards.title: A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100. The symbol % reads "percent", and x% is by definition equal to x/100. Thus 25% = 25/100 = 1/4, 8% = 8/100 = 2/25, and 100% = 100/100 = 1, the whole. The word comes from the Latin per centum, "per hundred": a percentage answers the question "how many out of every hundred?" Three connected views of the same number make percentages flexible:
1. As a fraction: x% = x/100, which then simplifies like any fraction (35% = 35/100 = 7/20). Going the other way, any fraction a/b can be re-written with denominator 100 (multiply numerator and denominator by 100/b when it divides evenly, or divide a by b and multiply by 100) to give its percentage form: 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%.
2. As a ratio: x% is exactly the ratio x: 100. This links directly back to the ratio work of this chapter — a percentage is the special ratio whose second term has been standardised to 100, which is precisely why two percentages can be compared at a glance even when the underlying totals differ.
3. As a decimal: because dividing by 100 shifts the decimal point two places left, x% = x ÷ 100; 45% = 0.45, 6% = 0.06, 120% = 1.2. Converting back, multiply by 100 (shift two places right). Two working rules follow from the definition. To find x% of a quantity N, compute N × x/100 — for example, 20% of 250 = 250 × 20/100 = 50. To find what percent A is of B, compute A/B × 100 — for example, what percent is 45 of 200? 45/200 × 100 = 22.5%. Percentages may exceed 100 whenever the part exceeds the comparison total (a jar holding 150% of its labelled capacity is overfull by half), and "100%" always means the entire quantity under discussion.
steps: A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is permanently fixed at 100 — and that single design decision is why percentages exist at all: they trade away a fraction's flexibility to buy instant comparison, so the…
Argument 1 — why fix the denominator at 100?
Fractions with different denominators are hard to compare: which is bigger, 17/40 of the class or 11/25?
You must bring them to a common denominator (and 40 and 25 share 200) before deciding.
But re-express both as out-of-a-hundred — 42.5% against 44% — and the comparison is instant.
Every shop discount board, exam result and battery indicator uses percentages for exactly this reason: one fixed denominator turns all comparisons into comparing whole numbers.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 35% written as 1/35 or as the decimal 35.0) reveals the exact misconception that the % sign is a decoration rather than an instruction — the sign is a standing instruction to divide by 100, so stripping it without dividing corrupts the…
remember: Define percentage in your own words and write 35% (i) as a fraction in simplest form, (ii) as a decimal.
Convert each: (a) 3/4 to a percent, (b) 0.06 to a percent, (c) 9/25 to a percent, (d) 150% to a fraction in simplest form.
Ravi argues: "60% means 60 out of 100, so you can only take 60% of something if you have at least 100 of it. 60% of 30 mangoes is impossible." Is Ravi….

cards.title: Speed is the distance travelled in one unit of time…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
Speed is the distance travelled in one unit of time — a rate that compares a distance with the time taken to cover it. Speed = Distance ÷ Time. A bus that covers 180 km in 4 hours has speed 180 ÷ 4 = 45 km per hour, written 45 km/h: in every hour of the journey (as long as the speed stays steady), 45 km are covered. Speed carries a compound unit — a distance unit joined to a time unit by "per": kilometres per hour (km/h), metres per second (m/s), metres per minute (m/min). The word "per" signals division, exactly as it did in the unitary method (value per one item): 45 km/h literally means 45 ÷ 1 (km per hour). Because of this, the three quantities obey a three-way relationship:
- Speed = Distance ÷ Time
- Distance = Speed × Time
- Time = Distance ÷ Speed Knowing any two of the three quantities determines the third. A runner at a steady 8 m/s for 12 seconds covers 8 × 12 = 96 m; to cover 200 m at that pace takes 200 ÷ 8 = 25 s. Two cautions anchor the definition. First, units must match before dividing: distance in km with time in hours gives km/h; distance in metres with time in seconds gives m/s — never divide km by minutes and keep both labels. Converting first (km to m, hours to minutes or seconds) is part of the computation, not an extra. Second, the formula assumes uniform speed — the same distance covered in every equal slice of time. Real traffic rarely holds one speed; when a journey's speed varies, the single speed computed by total distance ÷ total time describes the journey as a whole (a smoother idea treated more fully in later classes), while this node's problems state or imply steady speeds.
steps: Speed is the unitary method applied to motion — divide the journey by the time it took to find "how far per one hour", and every speed question in daily life, from catching a school bus to planning a train trip…

Argument 1 — speed is a rate, and "per" is its engine. 45 km/h is a complete sentence: "45 kilometres for every 1 hour." This is the same structure as ₹30 per kg or 60% per hundred from the previous nodes; the only…
Whenever you see "per" in mathematics, reach for division; the word was designed to point at it. Argument 2 — one relationship, three doors.
From Speed = Distance ÷ Time, the two rearrangements follow: Distance = Speed × Time and Time = Distance ÷ Speed.

Do not memorise three facts — memorise one and re-derive the others by the flip logic: if distance = speed × time, then covering 60 km at 30 km/h must take 60 ÷ 30 = 2 h, and running 8 m/s for 12 s must cover 8 × 12 =…
To quote km/h, first convert 10 minutes to 1/6 hour (or 5 km to 5000 m and compare metres per minute), then divide: 5 ÷ (1/6) = 30 km/h.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3 ÷ 36 = 1/12 "km/h") reveals the misconception that speed is simply "time over distance" because the words occur in that order in the sentence — the division must always be distance in the numerator divided by time, since speed counts…
remember: Define speed and state its formula. A boy cycles 36 km in 3 hours at a steady pace. Find his speed in km/h.
A train moves at a uniform 60 km/h. How long will it take to cover 240 km? Show the formula used and the working.
Evaluate this claim: "A car whose speedometer reads 80 km/h must travel exactly 80 km every hour of its journey." Is the claim fully….

cards.title: Time and distance work rests on one locked relationship among three quantities…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Time and distance work rests on one locked relationship among three quantities — Speed = Distance ÷ Time — and the whole topic is the art of opening this relationship from any two of its sides. The rearranged forms Distance = Speed × Time and Time = Distance ÷ Speed are not new facts but the same equation read from different doors, as introduced in; this node consolidates that machinery and extends it in two directions. First, multi-leg journeys. A real outing is a chain of legs, each with its own distance and speed, plus halts that consume time but no distance. The governing bookkeeping is: total distance = sum of the legs' distances; total time = sum of the legs' times plus the halts; and each leg's time is found from its own numbers by Time = Distance ÷ Speed. Second, average speed for a whole journey is DEFINED as total distance covered ÷ total time taken (halts included). For a scooter that runs 24 km in the first half hour and 18 km in the next half hour, the average is (24 + 18) ÷ 1 h = 42 km/h. The definition matters because the average of a journey is NOT usually the average of the two speeds: a car doing 40 km/h out and 60 km/h back over equal 120 km stretches averages 240 km ÷ 5 h = 48 km/h, not 50 — the slower leg hogs more time, dragging the true average toward it. Units remain the gatekeeper: minutes must become fractions of an hour (45 min = 3/4 h; 20 min = 1/3 h) before meeting km/h speeds, and metres must become kilometres (or seconds to hours) before units can be quoted. Every answer is checked by re-substitution — rebuild one given quantity from the computed ones and confirm it matches.
steps: A journey is a chain of legs, and the arithmetic of the whole journey is strict bookkeeping over the legs: distances ADD, times ADD (halts included), and any "average" must be earned by dividing the added distance by…
Argument 1 — the one equation, used in all three directions, is the entry ticket.
Before multi-leg work, the three-door fluency must be automatic: 210 km in 3.5 h → speed 60 km/h (divide); 60 km/h for 3.5 h → 210 km (multiply); 210 km at 60 km/h → 3.5 h (divide the other way).
In this node the doors are opened with messier numbers — 1 h 45 min as 1.75 h, 8000 m as 8 km — so unit conversion stops being a separate topic and becomes a step inside every computation.
Argument 2 — legs are computed separately, then added.

A trip of 24 km at 48 km/h, a 20-minute chai halt, then 18 km at 36 km/h is THREE mini-problems: leg times 0.5 h and 0.5 h, halt 1/3 h. Totals: 42 km, and 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/2 = 4/3 h = 1 h 20 min. The discipline is refusing…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 210 ÷ 3.30 = 63.6 by reading "3:30" as 3.30, or 210 ÷ 3 = 70 by ignoring the minutes entirely) reveals the misconception that clock notation is decimal — 0.30 of an hour is 18 minutes, not 30; the minutes must be divided by 60 and ADDED…
remember: State the three forms of the speed–distance–time relationship. A bus covers 210 km in 3 hours 30 minutes. Find its speed in km/h.
A cyclist rides at a uniform 15 km/h.….
Arjun claims: "My car did 40 km/h going to Meerut and 60 km/h coming back, so my average speed for the round trip was 50 km/h." The one-way distance is 120 km. Compute the true….

cards.title: Building on children’s previous learning means explicitly linking the new ideas…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Building on children’s previous learning means explicitly linking the new ideas of ratio and proportion to concepts already mastered: (1) Fractions – a fraction (a)/(b) describes a part of a whole; a ratio a:b compares two separate quantities, but both use the same numerator‑denominator structure. (2) Multiplication and division – scaling a recipe (multiply both terms) or finding a unit rate (divide) are direct applications of the multiplication tables and division facts learned in earlier classes. (3) Comparison language – “more than”, “less than”, “twice as many” are verbal forms of ratio that students have used in word problems on addition and subtraction. (4) Measurement units – length, mass, capacity problems in Class 4‑5 required converting units using multiplication/division; the same operations appear when solving speed‑time‑distance problems later in this chapter. The node does not introduce new algorithms; it only makes these connections visible so that the formal definitions in sibling nodes ( to) feel like natural extensions rather than isolated rules.
steps: Ratio and proportion grow naturally from the fractions, multiplication, and comparison skills students already know.

Here is why: first, a fraction (3)/(5) tells “3 parts out of 5 equal parts of one whole”; a ratio 3:5 tells “3 parts of one quantity for every 5 parts of another quantity” — the symbols are identical but the referents…
Second, when a recipe says “2 cups rice for 3 cups water”, doubling the recipe uses the multiplication fact 2×2=4 and 3×2=6; the same multiplication tables memorised in Class 3 do the work.
Third, finding how much rice for 1 cup water (unitary method) is just division 2÷3, a division fact practised since Class 4.
Fourth, everyday language — “Rohan has twice as many marbles as Meena” — is a verbal ratio that students have turned into addition/subtraction problems earlier; now they learn to write it as 2:1.
Consider a classroom activity: give each group 20 beads, ask them to split into two colours in the ratio 3:2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “decimals”) reveals the misconception that ratio notation is a new symbol system unrelated to prior fraction work.
remember: Which earlier mathematical concept is most directly used when writing a ratio as a fraction.
Explain how the idea of equal sharing (division) helps in understanding the unitary method.
A student says the ratio 3:4 is the same as the fraction (3)/(4). Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Presenting situations that prompt children to form patterns and feel the need…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Presenting situations that prompt children to form patterns and feel the need for a symbol in place of a number is a pedagogical strategy that bridges concrete arithmetic and abstract algebraic thinking. In Class 6, students encounter repeated contexts — sharing sweets, mixing paint colours, comparing distances — where the same numerical relationship recurs. By deliberately varying the numbers while keeping the underlying structure constant, the teacher guides learners to recognise a stable pattern (e.g., “total ÷ groups = share per group”). Once the pattern is evident, the inconvenience of writing the full arithmetic sentence repeatedly creates a natural demand for a concise notation. This notation evolves into the ratio symbol “:” and later into the proportion sign “::”. The approach connects directly to the sibling concepts: the difference between fraction and ratio, the concept of ratio, proportion as equality of two ratios, unitary method, word problems, percent as fraction with denominator 100, and speed‑time‑distance (,). The strategy also builds on children’s previous learning and prepares them for hands‑on exploration with the Maths Kit.
steps: The one thing students must remember is that a symbol becomes useful only when a pattern repeats across many situations, because it lets us write the relationship once and apply it everywhere.
Here is why: first, patterns appear naturally when we share things equally — whether it is 12 mangoes among 3 friends, 20 pencils among 4 boxes, or 15 rotis among 5 people.
Second, each situation can be described by the same arithmetic sentence “total ÷ groups = share”, but writing it repeatedly is tedious.
Third, when we notice the pattern, we can invent a shorthand like “total: groups = share: 1” to capture the rule in one line.
Fourth, this shorthand works for any numbers, so we can solve new problems instantly — for example, 30 candies among 6 children becomes 30:6 = 5:1, giving 5 candies each.
Fifth, the same idea extends to mixing paint (2 parts red: 3 parts blue) or comparing speeds (60 km in 1 hour = 60:1).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Symbols are only for algebra”) reveals the misconception that symbols are abstract decorations rather than tools for generalising arithmetic patterns.
remember: A student says, “I can just keep doing the division each time; I don’t need a special symbol.” What does this reveal about the student’s understanding of patterns.
In a class activity, children divide 18 marbles into 2, 3, and 6 equal….
Evaluate the claim: “Using a symbol like ‘:’ is only useful when numbers are large; for small numbers we can just count.”.

cards.title: The Maths Kit for Ratio and Proportion is a curated collection of concrete…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Maths Kit for Ratio and Proportion is a curated collection of concrete manipulatives and activity cards designed to make the abstract ideas of ratio, proportion, unitary method, percent, and speed-time-distance tangible for Class 6 learners. It includes: (1) coloured counters or beads in multiple hues to represent quantities in a given ratio; (2) graduated measuring tapes and rulers to explore direct variation in length, weight, and capacity; (3) double‑number‑line strips and proportion tables that visually demonstrate equality of two ratios; (4) unitary‑method cards showing step‑by‑step breakdown of “value of one unit” leading to “value of required units”; (5) percent‑grid sheets (10 × 10 squares) to model percent as a fraction with denominator 100; (6) speed‑time‑distance scenario cards with simple daily‑life contexts (e.g., a cycle ride to school, a bus journey). The kit links directly to the sibling concept nodes: it provides the physical embodiment of “Concept of Ratio”, “Proportion as equality of two ratios”, “Unitary method”, “Word problems on ratio and proportions”, “Idea of percent as fraction with 100 as denominator”, and “Idea of speed and simple daily life problems related to speed, time and distance” (,). By manipulating the kit, students build patterns, recognise the need for symbols, and connect prior learning (,) to formal notation.
steps: The Maths Kit turns ratio and proportion into a hands‑on experience so that every learner can see, touch, and reason with the relationships before writing symbols.
Here is why: concrete materials bridge the gap between everyday comparisons (like sharing laddoos) and the formal notation of ratio and proportion.

First, the coloured counters let students physically group items in a given ratio, say 3: 2, by placing three red beads and two blue beads repeatedly; they then count total groups to discover equivalent ratios such as…
Second, the double‑number‑line strips provide a visual proof that two ratios are equal — when the marks for 3: 2 and 6: 4 line up, students see proportion as alignment rather than a rule to memorise.

Third, the unitary‑method cards break a problem like “5 pens cost ₹75, find cost of 8 pens” into “cost of 1 pen = ₹75 ÷ 5 = ₹15” and then “cost of 8 pens = 8 × ₹15 = ₹120”, reinforcing direct variation step by step.
Fourth, the percent‑grid sheet (100 squares) makes “25 %” literally 25 shaded squares out of 100, so the fraction 25/100 and decimal 0.25 become obvious.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is used to measure length in centimetres”) reveals the misconception that the strip is a measuring tool rather than a proportional reasoning aid.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the double‑number‑line strip in the Maths Kit for Ratio and Proportion.
A student uses the coloured counters to model the ratio 4: 3 by placing 4 red and 3 blue….
Using the unitary‑method card, a student solves: “If 6 notebooks cost ₹180, what is the cost of 10 notebooks?” They write: “Cost of 1 notebook = 180 ÷ 6 =….

cards.title: A constant is a number whose value is fixed…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A constant is a number whose value is fixed — it is the same in every situation, every example and every row of every table. In the rule "add 5 to a number", the 5 is a constant: whether you start from 2, from 50 or from 1000, the rule always adds exactly 5. In the statement "every square has 4 sides", the 4 is a constant: every square, drawn anywhere, of any size, has exactly 4 sides. Constants are written as ordinary numerals (2, 7, 0.5, 100) — their whole identity is their fixed value. Three properties pin the idea down:
1. Same value everywhere: a constant does not depend on the situation it appears in. The 12 in "a year has 12 months" is the same 12 whether the year is 2019 or 2026, whether it is written on a blackboard in Kolkata or a calendar in Kochi.
2. Independent of the case being considered: when we look at many examples (many squares, many weeks, many auto-rickshaws), a constant is the number that refuses to change across all the cases — it is exactly what the "changeless column" of a comparison table shows.
3. Contrast with what can change: a constant only means something against a background of things that CAN vary — the number of sides of a shape is constant for squares, while the number of students present in a class can change daily. This node plants the fixed side of that contrast; the changing side (variables and unknowns) is developed in the next nodes ( onwards). Constants also live inside rules and patterns: in "start at 3 and keep adding 4", the starting point 3 and the step 4 are both constants of the pattern, while the terms 3, 7, 11, 15,... keep growing. Naming the constants of a rule is the first step towards writing the rule in algebraic form later in this chapter.
steps: A constant is a number with one job — to stay the same — and the entire skill of this node is the classification test that question asks: across every case you are shown, does this quantity hold one fixed value, or can…
Argument 1 — constants are the anchors that make facts worth learning.
"A triangle has 3 sides" is a usable fact precisely because the 3 never wobbles: triangle in a textbook, triangle cut from paper, triangle the size of a field — always 3.
When a quantity is constant, one sentence covers every case forever; that is why school facts (7 days a week, 12 months a year, 60 minutes an hour) are all constants.
The fixedness IS the usefulness.
Argument 2 — the classification test is "across cases".
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a constant is any big number like 100" or giving "the number of students in my class" as an example) reveals the misconception that "constant" describes a size or a personal fact rather than a property of fixedness — the definition is…
remember: Define a constant and give three examples of constants from daily life, stating the fixed value in each.
A number pattern follows the rule "start at 6 and keep adding….
Ravi claims: "The number of days in February is a constant, because February always has 28 days." Evaluate his claim….

cards.title: A variable is a symbol — usually a letter such as n, x or m…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A variable is a symbol — usually a letter such as n, x or m — that stands for a number which is free to change or is not yet known. In the rule "each of n children gets 3 toffees, so we need 3 × n toffees", the letter n is a variable: n = 5 describes one day's case (15 toffees), n = 30 another (90 toffees), and the single expression 3 × n covers every possible class size at once. An unknown is the twin idea: when a number is hidden but fixed by a condition ("a crate held some mangoes; after 12 more were added there were 45 — how many at the start?"), the letter m stands for that one hidden value until the condition pins it down (m + 12 = 45, so m = 33). Three properties frame the idea:
1. A variable names a slot, not a single thing: unlike a constant, whose one value never moves, a variable may take many values across cases — or one value that we discover, in the unknown case.
2. Context fixes the values: in a given problem, the letter's allowed values come from the situation (n counts children, so n = 1, 2, 3,...); the same letter can mean different things in different problems.
3. Variables make rules general: writing "7 × n" for the pattern 7, 14, 21, 28,... states the whole pattern in one line — this is the generalisation power that letters buy, and it is why algebra exists. This node introduces variables through patterns and through simple word problems; the pattern of sums of odd numbers begins here with 1 + 3 = 2 × 2 and grows through the next nodes.
steps: A variable is a letter employed as a container for a number that either changes from case to case or is hiding until a condition reveals it — and the fastest way to feel why letters are worth inventing is to try, once…

Try saying "the number of toffees needed is 3 multiplied by the number of children, whatever that is, for every group in the school, for any group that ever comes." One breath, and the sentence is already straining.
Now write 3 × n. The letter compresses an ocean of cases into three symbols — and unlike the sentence, the expression can be calculated with, checked, and later built upon.
Letters are not mathematical decoration; they are load-bearing shorthand for "any value this slot can hold".
Argument 2 — patterns hand the variable its first job. Look at 7, 14, 21, 28,...
Ask "which table is this?" — the 7 times table.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "n must be the number 3, since 3 is written in the expression") reveals the misconception that the printed digit is the moving part and the letter is decoration — the roles are exactly reversed: 3 is the constant (same every case), n is…
remember: Define a variable and an unknown in one sentence each. In "3 × n toffees for n children", which idea does n play — the free variable or the locked unknown.
The pattern 7, 14, 21, 28,... continues. (a) State the rule in words. (b) Write the rule using a letter for the term position. (c) Use your rule to write the 10th term.
Ravi says: "x is called a variable, but in my sum x = 5, so x is really just the number 5 and variables are pointless." Evaluate his claim in two or three sentences, using at….

cards.title: This node studies the staircase of odd-number sums: 1 = 1 × 1…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
This node studies the staircase of odd-number sums: 1 = 1 × 1, 1 + 3 = 4 = 2 × 2, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3 × 3, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4 × 4. Each rung adds the next odd number (the odd numbers go 1, 3, 5, 7,..., each 2 more than the one before), and each running total turns out to be a square number — the count of odd numbers added, multiplied by itself. The two moving parts have names:
- n — the variable counting HOW MANY odd numbers have been added (from the previous node): n = 3 in 1 + 3 + 5.
- the running total — the sum so far, which equals n × n at every rung. The pattern's law, observed rung by rung: after adding the first n odd numbers, the total is n × n. This is verified here case by case (n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6,...) with every addition shown; the complete generalisation — why it must work for EVERY n — is assembled in the next node. A second face of the same fact: each new rung climbs exactly one square, and the climb size (4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7) is itself the next odd number — that is WHY adding odd numbers walks along the squares.
steps: Adding consecutive odd numbers walks exactly along the square numbers — 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 — because each step's climb (3, 5, 7,...) IS the odd number being added, and the entire pattern can be generated, checked and run…
Argument 1 — the staircase, built honestly.
No skipping: 1 = 1 × 1.
Then 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3 × 3 (adding 5 to 4).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 written as 5 × 5 "because 5 was the last number added") reveals the exact misconception this pattern punishes — squaring the LAST ODD NUMBER instead of counting the TERMS: the last addend 7 contributed the climb to the next…
remember: Compute 1 + 3 + 5 and write the answer in "n × n" form. Then compute 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 the same way, showing the running addition.
Without adding all five numbers, state the value of 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9, and justify the shortcut in one sentence. Then verify by stepwise addition.
Ravi claims: "1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 11 × 11 = 121, since 11 is the last number in the sum." Is Ravi….

cards.title: The generalisation of the odd-number staircase states…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
The generalisation of the odd-number staircase states: the sum of the first n odd numbers equals n × n, written compactly as n². In symbols: 1 + 3 + 5 +... + (2n − 1) = n². Three pieces of the statement deserve exact attention:
1. The letter n (from) is the count of odd numbers added — a counting number 1, 2, 3,... The law holds for EVERY counting number n, not just the rows verified so far.
2. 2n − 1 is the nth odd number — a formula for the odd numbers themselves: the 1st odd is 2(1) − 1 = 1, the 4th is 2(4) − 1 = 7, the 20th is 39. This tells you where any rung's sum STOPS without listing all the odds.
3. n² (read "n squared") is shorthand for n × n — the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25,... are exactly 1², 2², 3², 4², 5²,.... Why the law always holds (the engine, in numbers): each new odd number lifts the total from one square to the next. From 9 = 3², adding 7 (which is 2 × 3 + 1) lands on 16 = 4²; from 16, adding 9 = 2 × 4 + 1 lands on 25 = 5². In dots: an n × n square, given an L-shaped border of 2n + 1 new dots, becomes the (n+1) × (n+1) square. Since the staircase starts on a square (1 = 1²) and every step lands on the next square, it can never leave the squares — that is the complete reason, and will reuse this pattern-building machinery on new families.
steps: The staircase law — the first n odd numbers always total n² — is not a lucky run of rows but a locked mechanism: every odd number is exactly the gap between two consecutive squares, so a walk that adds odds in order…
Argument 1 — the law in full dress.
Write it once, precisely: 1 + 3 + 5 +... + (2n − 1) = n².
The ending 2n − 1 is the nth odd number — the rung where an n-term sum naturally stops (n = 6 stops at 2 × 6 − 1 = 11; n = 20 stops at 39).
With this line, every forwards question is one multiplication: 20 odd numbers? 20² = 400.
Every backwards question is one square-table hunt: total 225?
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., answering 9 × 9 = 81 "since 9 is the largest odd in the sum") reveals the persistent count-versus-last-odd confusion — the law's input is HOW MANY odd numbers (5), never how big the final one is; the position labels 1st through 5th under…
remember: State the staircase generalisation in words and in symbols. Then use it: what is 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9, and why does the answer follow without adding.
Use the law to find: (a) the sum of the first 20 odd numbers; (b) the 20th odd number; (c) check the last rung of your (a) answer using 19² and the 20th odd number.
Shalini says: "Patterns in maths always break eventually — this odd-numbers-equal-squares trick will break by the 15th row." Evaluate her claim: test the 15th row fully, and state….

cards.title: A pattern in mathematics is a sequence of numbers, shapes…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A pattern in mathematics is a sequence of numbers, shapes, or objects that follows a predictable rule. Generating patterns with more examples and generalisation involves observing several instances of a pattern, identifying the underlying relationship between the position (often denoted by n) and the value, and expressing that relationship as an algebraic formula. For instance, the sequence of odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7,… can be generalised as the nth odd number = 2n − 1, and the sum of the first n odd numbers = n². Other common patterns include arithmetic progressions where each term increases by a constant difference d, giving the general term Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d (a = first term). Geometric patterns, such as matchstick squares, also yield linear formulas. The process connects arithmetic observation to algebraic representation: constants (fixed numbers), variables (n representing any natural number), and operations (addition, multiplication) combine to form an expression that predicts any term without listing all previous ones. This node builds on the earlier recognition that the sum of odd numbers equals n² (node) and extends it to creating and generalising new patterns, laying groundwork for framing algebraic expressions and solving simple equations in subsequent nodes.
steps: The key takeaway is that any pattern with a steady rule can be captured by a single algebraic formula using n, allowing us to jump straight to any term.
Here is why: patterns appear everywhere — from the steps of a staircase to the arrangement of seeds in a sunflower — and algebra gives us a compact language to describe them.
First, we identify the pattern type: if each term increases by the same amount, it is an arithmetic pattern.
For example, the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15… adds 4 each time.
The first term a = 3, common difference d = 4, so the nth term is Tₙ = 3 + (n − 1)×4 = 4n − 1.
Second, we test the formula: for n = 1, T₁ = 3; n = 2, T₂ = 7; matches the given terms.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., n(n+1)/2) reveals the misconception that the student is confusing the sum of odd numbers with the sum of the first n natural numbers.
remember: What is the general formula for the sum of the first n odd natural numbers.
The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, … follows a constant difference. Write the nth term formula.
A student claims the pattern 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, … has the general term n² + 1. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: An unknown is a number that is hiding but fixed…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
An unknown is a number that is hiding but fixed: the situation itself pins down exactly one value for it, and a letter (m, p, t,...) holds its place until the value is caught. The node met the unknown as the "locked" cousin of the variable; this node turns unknown-hunting into a systematic skill using simple contexts with a single operation — stories whose condition uses only one of the four operations. Every hunt has three stations:
1. The letter-condition: translate the story into one line with the letter, e.g., "some students; 17 more board the bus; then 53" becomes c + 17 = 53. The story's verb (boarded = added, dropped = subtracted, rows of equal size = multiplied, shared equally = divided) chooses the operation — the condition is written, not guessed.
2. The undoing move: each operation has an inverse that undoes it — addition undoes subtraction and vice versa; multiplication undoes division and vice versa. Because the condition has only ONE operation, exactly ONE undoing move releases the unknown: c = 53 − 17 = 36.
3. The forwards check: replay the story with the caught value (36 + 17 = 53 ✓). The check converts a confident guess into a certified answer and exposes every wrong direction. Pattern rules from the previous nodes hand out unknowns ready-made. The rule "each term of a pattern is 9 × n" (,) becomes a hunt when a term is named: 9 × n = 117, so n = 117 ÷ 9 = 13 — the 13th position. The odd-number law of runs backwards the same way: a total of 121 must be 11 × 11, so eleven odd numbers were added. What this node does NOT yet do is solve two-step conditions or use formal balancing methods — that machinery waits for; and the naming of an expression's parts (literal numbers, terms, coefficients) begins in.
steps: An unknown is caught with one undoing move: write the letter-condition, invert the single operation the story performed, and certify the catch with a forwards check — three stations, in that order, every time.
Argument 1 — the condition comes first because the verb chooses the operation.
"17 more boarded" is an addition story;
"9 degrees dropped" is a subtraction story;
"7 equal rows" is a multiplication story;
"shared equally" is a division story.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., m = 60 − 5 = 55, or "m could be any number because letters are free") reveals the twin misconception that undoing means subtracting regardless of the operation, and that every letter ranges freely — the condition 5 × m = 60 is a lock…
remember: Define an unknown in one sentence. In the condition 5 × m = 60, state which role m plays, find m, and check forwards.
A pattern follows the rule "each term is 6 × n". (a) Write its first five terms. (b) Name the position that holds the term 96: write the condition, undo, and check.
Ravi solves p − 9 = 14 like this: "undo minus 9, so subtract 9 again: p = 14 − 9 = 5." Evaluate his move, give the correct solution, and demonstrate the check on both answers.

cards.title: A literal number (also called a literal) is a letter of the alphabet — a, b…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A literal number (also called a literal) is a letter of the alphabet — a, b, c,..., x, y, z — used in algebra to stand for a number. The word "literal" itself announces the idea: it comes from "letter". Where a numeral (7, 25, 0.5) shows its value on its face, a literal number is a NUMBERS-stand-in: it holds a place for a value that the situation supplies — a count that changes (n children), a hidden value to be caught (m + 12 = 45), or any number whatsoever when a law is being stated (a + b = b + a). Three properties pin the term down:
1. A literal denotes a number, not a thing or a word. In "6 × b students", the literal b stands for the NUMBER of benches, not for benches or the word "bench". This is the single most-tested distinction of the term.
2. Within one expression or problem, the same literal holds one value. In a × a, both a's are the same number (a × a = a²); in a × b, a and b may hold different values because they are different literals. Scope is per problem: the same letter may hold different values in different problems (the literal c held 36 students in one hunt of and 77 coupons in another — each problem owns its letter).
3. Literals make laws writable. Rules such as "any number plus any number, in either order, gives the same total" collapse into one line with literals: a + b = b + a. Without literals, generality needs strained sentences; with them, one line covers every case — the very reason algebra exists. Notation conventions ride along with literals: the multiplication sign is dropped between literals and numerals — 7 × n is written 7n, a × b is written ab, a × a is written a² (read "a squared"); the numeral is placed first (m × 9 is written 9m). A convention of usage (not a rule of mathematics) prefers letters from the early alphabet (a, b, c) for known numbers and letters from the later alphabet (x, y, z) for unknowns — the hunts of used whatever letter fitted the story (c for coupons, s for stalls), which is always permitted. This node NAMES the letter for the first time; the nodes that follow dissect what the letter builds — terms, factors and coefficients ( onwards).
steps: A literal number is a letter doing a number's job — the alphabet's formal entry into mathematics — and the whole skill of this node is naming it precisely, so that every later discussion of expressions has a word for…
Argument 1 — the name closes an old loop.
Since the class has used letters freely: n counted odd numbers, m hid mangoes, c counted coupons.
But the letter itself never got its name.
"Literal number" is that name: a letter EMPLOYED AS A NUMBER.

The definition is worth memorising word for word because every wrong reading of algebra later — "x is a word", "x is a box with nothing in it", "x is a shape" — dies against the precise phrase "a letter that stands for…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a literal number is a letter that stands for a word or an object, like b stands for benches") reveals the misconception that literals denote things — a literal denotes a NUMBER (the number of benches); confusing the number with the…
remember: Define a literal number and give three examples of literals from expressions you have already met. Why does algebra need them at all.
Consider the expression 7 × n from the pattern 7, 14….
Ravi claims: "A literal number is a letter that stands for a WORD — like m stands for 'mangoes'." Evaluate his claim and repair it with the correct statement, using the condition….

cards.title: A term is one part of an algebraic expression…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A term is one part of an algebraic expression, set off from the other parts by the + or − signs. An expression is built by joining terms: 7n + 5 has two terms (7n and 5); 3a + 2b − 4c has three terms (3a, 2b and −4c); the lone numeral 7 is itself a one-term expression. Each term is a compact product of numerals and literals ('s literal numbers) — 7n is the numeral 7 times the literal n — or a single numeral standing alone. Four properties fix the idea:
1. The signs are the walls. Reading left to right, every stretch between two sign-walls is one term. A term may hold many factors INSIDE it (7xy is one term holding three factors) — fullness inside never splits a term; only a + or − wall does.
2. The sign travels with the term. In 2a − 3b, the terms are 2a and −3b: the minus belongs to the 3b, because the expression says "take 2a and then take away three b's". Reading every expression as a SUM of signed terms (2a + (−3b)) is what makes this exact.
3. Constant term versus literal term. A term with no literal (5, −9) is a constant term — it never moves; a term carrying a literal (4x, −2m) takes the value its literal is given. Many real bills mix both: fare = 25 + 12k has the constant term 25 (the base) and the literal term 12k (the part that moves with k).
4. Terms are counted, then handled one at a time. To evaluate an expression, each term is evaluated first and the results are then joined by the signs: 7n + 5 at n = 4 is 7 × 4 + 5 = 28 + 5 = 33. What this node does NOT yet do: name the factors inside a term, classify expressions by term-count, or gather terms that look alike. Here the skill is to SEE the terms — the plate, the katoris, and what each holds.
steps: A term is an expression's katori: one dish per wall — and the entire skill of this node is seeing the walls, so that expressions stop being letter-soup and become assemblies of countable, evaluable parts.
Argument 1 — terms make expressions speakable.
Before this node, 7n + 5 was "an expression"; now it is TWO TERMS — a moving part and a fixed part.
That description is already an explanation: the 7n grows with the number of children, the 5 never moves, and the whole expression models any canteen bill of the shape "₹5 per item plus ₹5 fixed".
Terminology converts a mark on the board into a story with roles, which is exactly what the terminology chain (007 onward) is for: literal named the letters, terms name the blocks.
Argument 2 — the walls, not the letters, do the dividing.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "three terms: 3, a and 2b" or "four terms: 3, a, 2, b") reveals the misconception that the expression splits at every SYMBOL rather than only at the sign-walls — inside a term the numeral and literal are glued by multiplication (3a is…
remember: Define a term, and list all the terms of the expression 3a + 2b. How many terms are there, and what kind is each.
List the terms of 5x − 7 + 2y. (a) How many terms are there? (b) Which term is constant and what does that mean? (c) Why does the minus belong to the 7 and not to the 2y.
A student says: "7n + 5 has three terms, because 7, n and 5 are three separate things on the page." Evaluate this claim and give the correct count with the reason.

cards.title: An algebraic expression is a meaningful combination of numerals and literal…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
An algebraic expression is a meaningful combination of numerals and literal numbers joined by operation signs — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division — and carrying NO equals sign. Expressions are built from terms: 7n + 5 is the sum of two terms; 25 + 12k likewise; 4xy is a single-term expression. The recipe reading is exact: 7n + 5 means "seven times the literal, plus five" — every expression encodes an instruction, and evaluating it means carrying out the instruction once the literals are given values (n = 4: 7 × 4 + 5 = 33). Four boundaries shape the concept:
1. Expression versus equation. An expression is a phrase: 7n + 5 names a value once n is supplied, but makes NO claim. An equation — such as the hunt-conditions m + 12 = 45 of — is a sentence with an equals sign that CLAIMS two things are equal, and can be true or false, hunted or verified. Every condition of the earlier nodes was an equation built around expressions.
2. Meaningfulness. The signs must combine numerals and literals in a way arithmetic can execute: 5x + 3, 8 − z and a ÷ 2 are expressions; "x + +" is a string, not an expression — no instruction can be read from it.
3. Word order becomes operation order. Phrases translate into expressions with the words' order respected: "8 more than a number" is n + 8; "7 less than a number" is n − 7 (the number leads); "twice a number, then 5 added" is 2n + 5 — doubling happens FIRST because the words say so.
4. One expression, many values; one case, one value. Without a value for its literal, an expression stands ready for all cases (the whole point, from's two posters onward); once the literal is fixed, the expression yields exactly one value, computed term by term. This node names and handles the WHOLE; the next dissections go inside — factors and coefficients — and the solving of equations built from expressions waits for.
steps: An algebraic expression is a number-recipe with the meal left uncooked — numerals and literals joined by operations, no equals sign — and fluency with expressions is three skills in one coat: writing them from words…
Argument 1 — the missing equals sign is the definition's hinge.
Everything the chapter built before this either HUNTS (m + 12 = 45 — a claim, an equation) or GENERATES (7 × n — a recipe, an expression).
The equals sign is the border marker: with it, a line asserts and can be checked; without it, a line only instructs.
The distinction is worth a definition of its own because students otherwise treat 3x + 2 as "unsolved" — it is not unsolved; it is UNASKED.
Nothing is hidden in 3x + 2; it waits for an input, not for a detective.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "an equation is a longer expression" or "they are the same, the equals sign is just style") reveals the misconception that the equals sign is punctuation — it is a CLAIM marker: expressions can be evaluated, equations can be verified or…
remember: Define an algebraic expression, give two examples, and state precisely how an expression differs from an equation.
Translate each phrase into an expression: (a) "8 more than a number"; (b) "twice a number"; (c) "7 less than a number"; (d) "half of a number".
A student translates "a number increased by 5, then doubled" as 2n + 5. Evaluate the translation, give the correct expression, and demonstrate with n = 4 that the two disagree.

cards.title: A factor is one of the numerals or literals multiplied together to form a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A factor is one of the numerals or literals multiplied together to form a product. In the term 7n, the factors are 7 and n; in 4xy, the factors are 4, x and y; in a², the factors are a and a (the same literal written twice, because a number is multiplied by ITSELF). A term IS its factors' product: 7n means 7 × n, and every way the multiplication can be grouped or reordered still yields the same term. Four boundaries make the term precise:
1. Factors live INSIDE a term; terms live inside an expression. The levels nest: an expression is built of terms joined by + and − walls; each term is built of factors joined by multiplication. 6ab + 7 has two terms; the first term 6ab has three factors (6, a, b); the second term 7 has one factor (7).
2. Multiplication is the only glue. However crowded a term looks — 3p²q holds four factors (3, p, p, q) — no + or − ever appears inside; the walls outside and the glue inside are what the term/factor split means.
3. Numeral factors and literal factors. Every term with a numeral has exactly the numeral(s) it shows as its numeral factor(s), and every letter as a literal factor; 7n = one numeral factor (7) plus one literal factor (n). The special NAME of the numeral factor is the business of the next node.
4. Two senses of "factor" share the word. Factors of a NUMBER (arithmetic sense): the numbers that divide it exactly — the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of a TERM (algebra sense): the multiplicative building blocks listed above. Related but different jobs: 3 is a factor of the number 12 in the first sense, and one factor of the term 12n in the second; n is a factor of the term 12n but not a factor of the number 12. This node dissects; the next names — the numeral factor of a term gets its formal title (coefficient) in, and the classification of expressions by their term-structure comes in.
steps: A factor is one strand of a term's multiplication — the flour, sugar and ghee of the recipe — and the entire skill of this node is to open each katori ('s picture) and name what the multiplication mixed, without ever…
Argument 1 — the levels nest, and naming them is the chapter's map. Expression → terms → factors: 6ab + 7 is an expression; 6ab and 7 are its terms; 6, a, b (and 7 alone) are the factors.
Each level has its own joining: walls (+, −) between terms, glue (×) between factors.
Once the map is explicit, the classic confessions dissolve: "7 and n are two terms" fails because nothing separates them but glue;
"6ab is one factor" fails because crowding is not indivisibility.
The student who can draw the three levels of any expression owns its anatomy.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the factors of 8m are 8m" (one), or "8, m, and 8m — since all three appear") reveals the misconception that the whole term is its own factor-listing unit — factors are the PARTS BEFORE multiplication, and including the product itself in…
remember: Define a factor of a term, and list all the factors of (a) 8m; (b) 5xy.
(a) Write a² in its long dress and list its factors. (b) How many factors does x² have, and why does one letter produce two factors? (c) List the factors of 12pq.
A student claims: "The factors of the expression 7n + 5 are 7, n and 5." Untangle the levels: is the claim right, what are the correct statements at each level, and what error….

cards.title: The coefficient of a term is the numeral factor of that term…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
The coefficient of a term is the numeral factor of that term — the number part that multiplies the literal part. In 7n, the coefficient is 7; in 4xy, it is 4; in 12p²q, it is 12. The coefficient is the term's SIZE-SETTER: whatever the literals turn out to be, the coefficient decides how many of each the term carries (7n is seven n's, never six or eight). Five conventions pin the word down:
1. The sign travels with the coefficient. In −6m, the coefficient is −6, not 6 — the term is (−6) × m, and its minus belongs to it exactly as ruled for terms. A term's direction (growth or subtraction) lives in its coefficient's sign.
2. The hidden 1. A term with no visible numeral still has a coefficient: x = 1 × x, ab = 1 × ab, a² = 1 × a² — the coefficient is 1, unwritten because multiplying by 1 changes nothing ('s invisible-1 discussion, now formally titled).
3. Coefficient versus constant term. In 2x + 7, the coefficient of the literal term 2x is 2, while 7 is a constant TERM — a whole katori, not the numeral factor of one. The two words answer different questions and must never be swapped: coefficients live inside literal terms; constant terms stand alone.
4. Coefficient is one factor among several. Every coefficient is a factor of its term, but not every factor is a coefficient — only the numeral one earns the title; 4xy has factors 4, x, y and exactly one coefficient: 4.
5. A constant term's own case. For the lone numeral 5, the term is its own coefficient in the formal sense (5 = 5 × 1); usual practice simply reads it as a constant term and moves on — the word "coefficient" earns its keep on literal terms. This node completes the anatomy of the chain: expression → terms → factors → the numeral factor titled coefficient. What follows builds on the finished skeleton — classification by term-structure and the gathering of like terms.
steps: The coefficient is a term's numeral factor wearing its job title — the size-setter — and this node's whole skill is titling it precisely, so that coefficient, factor, term and constant stop being shuffled labels and…
Argument 1 — the title completes the map. The chain now reads without gaps: an expression is built of terms; terms are built of factors; among the factors, the numeral one is the coefficient.
In 12p²q: expression-part 12p²q; term 12p²q; factors 12, p, p, q; coefficient 12.

Every inspection question a board paper can ask about a term's interior now has a named answer, and the naming is what makes later rules (like-term collection, degree) statable at all. Argument 2 — the hidden 1 is the…
The trap runs both ways: a student who says "x has no coefficient" has mistaken an unprinted 1 for an absence; a student who writes "1x" everywhere has not yet earned the convention's economy.
The honest sentence is: the coefficient of x is 1, and algebra leaves it at home.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (c) answered 8 "since only the number matters", or (b) answered "4" by grabbing a digit that is not even in the term) reveals the two conventions this node polices: the sign is part of the coefficient (dropping it reverses the term's job…
remember: Define the coefficient of a term, and state the coefficients of: (a) 12k; (b) 5xy; (c) −8p.
State the coefficients of: (a) x; (b) ab; (c) a². (d) Why is the coefficient never written in these terms.
In the expression 2x + 7, a student points at the 7 and says "that is the coefficient." Untangle the levels: what is the 7, what is the actual coefficient, and why the two must….

cards.title: A polynomial in one variable x is an algebraic expression of the form…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A polynomial in one variable x is an algebraic expression of the form P(x)=a_nx^n+a_n-1x^n-1+ +a_1x+a_0 where n is a non‑negative integer (the degree of the polynomial), a_n,a_n-1,,a_1,a_0 are constants called coefficients, a_n≠0 (otherwise the degree would be lower), each term a_kx^k consists of a coefficient multiplied by the variable raised to a whole‑number exponent, only the operations of addition, subtraction and multiplication by constants are allowed; division by a variable or negative/fractional exponents are not part of a polynomial. A polynomial with one term is a monomial (e.g., 7x^3), two terms a binomial (e.g., x^2-4), three terms a trinomial (e.g., 2x^2+3x+1). The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent of the variable that appears with a non‑zero coefficient. Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication: the sum, difference or product of two polynomials is again a polynomial. This node builds on the earlier concepts of literal numbers, terms, coefficients and expressions (nodes 02_007‑02_011) and prepares the ground for the formal study of degree (node 02_013) and like/unlike terms (node 02_014).
steps: A polynomial is a sum of terms, each term being a constant multiplied by a variable raised to a whole‑number power.
Here is why: every algebraic expression we have built so far — like `5x`, `‑3y²`, `7` — fits this pattern, and the rules of arithmetic let us combine them without leaving the family of polynomials.
First, recognise the building blocks: a term such as `4x³` has coefficient `4` and exponent `3`.
A constant like `‑9` is also a term (it can be seen as `‑9x⁰`).
Second, write any polynomial in standard form by ordering terms from highest to lowest exponent; this makes the degree immediately visible.
Third, classify by counting terms: one term → monomial, two → binomial, three → trinomial, more → polynomial.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any expression with a variable is a polynomial, ignoring the exponent rule.
remember: Which of the following expressions is a polynomial in one variable? A) 3x^-2+5 B) 4x^3+2x-7 C) (2)/(x)+x^2 D) √(x)+3x.
Write the polynomial 7-3x^2+5x^4-x in standard form and state its degree.
Add the polynomials P(x)=2x^3-4x+5 and Q(x)=-x^3+3x^2+x-2. Give the result in standard form.

cards.title: The degree of a term (in one variable) is the number of times the variable…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
The degree of a term (in one variable) is the number of times the variable appears as a factor in it — the exponent of the variable. In 4x³ the variable x is multiplied three times (4 × x × x × x), so the degree is 3; in 7n it appears once, so the degree is 1; in a constant term like 9 the variable appears ZERO times, so the degree is 0. The degree of a polynomial is the highest of the degrees of its terms — the tallest climb in the whole tiffin carrier. The polynomial 4x³ − 7x + 9 carries terms of degree 3, 1 and 0, so its degree is 3. Three conventions pin the word down:
1. Degree counts self-multiplications, not size. The degree of 12c is 1 even though 12 is a big numeral — degree looks only at the variable's exponent, never at the coefficient. A constant term 150 has degree 0 not because it is small but because no variable multiplies itself inside it at all. Senior classes write 150 = 150x⁰, and that 0 is exactly this count — but at this level it is enough to say: no variable, degree 0.
2. Degree is read from the structure, not the page. A jumbled polynomial like 7 − 5x² + x⁴ − 2x must be inspected term by term (or set in standard form,) before its degree is announced — the answer here is 4, from the x⁴ term, which happens to sit third on the page. Page order is presentation; degree is anatomy.
3. Naming by degree completes the two-axis classification. Chapter node named expressions by their NUMBER of terms (monomial, binomial, trinomial); degree adds the second axis — degree 1 is called linear, degree 2 quadratic, degree 3 cubic. The two axes answer different questions and both apply at once: x² + 3x + 2 is a quadratic trinomial (degree 2, three terms), while 2x + 5 is a linear binomial. This node continues the chain: expression → terms (008) → factors (010) → coefficient (011) → polynomial families (012) → now each term's power-count and the family's tallest rung. What follows builds on it: like and unlike terms sort terms by their literal structure, for which degree is the first checkpoint.
steps: The degree of a polynomial is its tallest rung on the variable's ladder — the highest number of times the variable multiplies itself in any one term — and naming it is the act that lets every later algebra rule…
The chain now reads: expression → terms → factors → coefficient → families by term-count.
Degree hangs one more tag on each katori: how many times the variable climbs inside it. 4x³ → three climbs; −7x → one; 9 → none.
Then one number crowns the whole carrier: the tallest.
Standard form is the degree-revealer, because the tallest climber is placed first and every later term climbs less.
Argument 2 — degree is structural, never numeric.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (b) answered "8" or "no degree", or (c) answered 3 by reading the coefficient as the degree) reveals the two boundary slips this node polices: a constant's degree is 0 (the count of appearances is zero — it is not "missing"), and degree…
remember: Define the degree of a term, and state the degrees of: (a) 5x; (b) 8; (c) 3y².
For the polynomial 6a³ − 2a + 5: (a) state the degree of each….
A student says: "The constant term 9 has no degree, since degree needs a variable." Give the corrected statement, justify it as a COUNT, and explain why 9,000 has exactly the same….

cards.title: Two terms are like terms when their literal parts are identical…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
Two terms are like terms when their literal parts are identical — the same variable letters raised to the same powers. 7n, −3n and n are like (all carry the literal part n); 4x²y and −x²y are like (both carry x²y); 5m and 5m² are UNLIKE (same letter, different powers). Terms with different literal parts are unlike terms: 4x and 3y, x² and x, 6k and 2a. Coefficients and signs play no role in the classification — only the literal part decides. Four rules pin the classification down:
1. The literal part is the whole test. 12c and −5c are like (one carries 12 of c, the other −5 of c); 12c and 12d are unlike (same numeral, different posters). Reading the coefficient first is the classic error — the letters, and only the letters, decide the family.
2. Same letter is not enough — the degree is the first checkpoint. After, every term carries a rung count: 5m sits on rung 1, 5m² on rung 2. Different rungs mean different dishes, however much the letter repeats: m² is m × m, a different literal part from m. In single-variable work the checkpoint is exact: like terms are precisely the terms of the same degree on the same letter.
3. All constants form one family. 6, −3, 17 are like terms — each is a katori with no variable at all (degree 0,), and "no variable" is a perfectly good shared literal part. A page's constants always gather into one constant.
4. Gathering is the point of the sort. Like terms may be combined into a single like term whose coefficient is the sum of their coefficients: 7n − 3n + n = (7 − 3 + 1)n = 5n — note the hidden 1 uncovered in the lone n, and the hidden −1 in any lone −n. Unlike terms can never merge: 4x + 3y simply stays 4x + 3y (it does NOT become 7xy). Gathering changes the page, never the value — at every substitution the gathered and original expressions agree, because pouring three katoris of rice into one leaves the meal unchanged. This node is the working payoff of the anatomy: terms (008), factors (010), coefficients (011), families (012) and degree (013) all feed the sort. What follows uses it: framing expressions from words produces jumbled pages precisely so that this node's sort can tidy them.
steps: Like terms are terms holding the same dish — the same literal part — and the whole skill of this node is the sort: identify the families, pour each family into one katori, and leave unlike katoris standing, with the…
Argument 1 — the sort is the anatomy's payoff.
The chain built everything this node needs: terms are katoris (008), each holds factors (010) with a numeral called the coefficient (011), and each literal sits on a degree rung (013).
Now the page asks its most practical question: which katoris hold the same dish?
The answer ignores the coefficients and signs entirely — 7n, −3n and n are one family in sizes 7, −3 and 1 — and reads only the literal part.
This is why the earlier nodes insisted on separating numeral from letter: the sort cannot even be attempted while "7n" is read as one indivisible blob.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calling (a) unlike "because of the minus", or (c) unlike "because k has no number") reveals the two slips this node polices: signs live on the coefficient and never break a family, and a missing numeral is a hidden 1, not a missing dish.
remember: Define like terms, and classify each pair as like or unlike with the reason: (a) 4x and −9x; (b) 4y and x²; (c) 6k and k; (d) 2m² and −5m².
Are the constant terms 6, −3 and 17 like terms? Justify with the degree reading, and gather them.
A student writes 5m + 5m² = 10m. Show the claim is false by the family test AND by a value-test at m = 2, and state exactly which checkpoint (from) catches it first.

cards.title: Framing an algebraic expression is translating a word statement into an…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
Framing an algebraic expression is translating a word statement into an expression: a letter (the chapter's poster for the unknown number) stands for the quantity, and each operation word is replaced by its operation. The chapter's translation dictionary: sum / more than / increased by / exceeds → +; difference / less than / decreased by / taken away from → −; product / times / of → ×; divided by / quotient / half of / one-third of → ÷. Framing has three hard rules:
1. Subtraction and division keep a strict order. Addition and multiplication can shuffle (y + 8 = 8 + y; 3 × n = n × 3), but subtraction and division cannot: "7 less than y" means y − 7 (start at y, go down 7) — writing 7 − y builds a different sentence. The sentence's LAST-stated quantity is often the one that must lead.
2. A phrase named as one unit goes in brackets. "3 times the sum of x and 2" multiplies 3 by the WHOLE sum: 3(x + 2). Framing it as 3x + 2 answers a different sentence ("3 times x, then 2 added"). The word "sum... multiplied" announces the bracket; the value-test exposes its absence (at x = 4: 18 against 14).
3. Declare the letter before using it. "Meena's age m; Ravi's age is 4 more than twice Meena's" begins by naming the poster: m = Meena's age, Ravi's age = 2m + 4. One letter, one meaning — using the same letter for two different quantities in one statement breaks the two-posters discipline of this chapter's variable frame.
A framed expression is checked by substituting an easy value and re-reading the sentence with that value — the arithmetic echo of the words. Framed pages then flow into the last node's work: 3x + 5x arrives and is gathered into 8x, and every framed term carries its coefficient and degree for the reading (,).
steps: Framing turns word statements into algebraic expressions by running the chapter's dictionary backwards — every operation word becomes its operation, every unnamed number becomes a declared letter — and the craft lives…
Argument 1 — the dictionary is the chapter's vocabulary, exercised.
Nodes 008–013 taught the anatomy of expressions; framing asks for the anatomy's construction: given the WORDS, build the page.
Sum → +, difference → −, product → ×, quotient → ÷ are the four load-bearing beams;
"more than", "increased by", "exceeds" are + in costume;
"less than", "decreased by", "taken away from" are − in costume;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (b) as 8 − k, (c) as p − 3 or 3p, (d) as 7 − 2q) reveals the order-and-dictionary slips this node exists to drill: "less than"/"taken away from" flip the sentence order onto the page, and "one-third of" divides — it neither subtracts nor…
remember: Frame each statement with a declared letter: (a) a number increased by 9; (b) 8 less than a number k; (c) one-third of a number p; (d) 7 taken away from twice a number q.
Translate each operation word into its operation, then frame: (a) "x exceeds….
A student frames "7 less than y" as 7 − y. Use the value-test at y = 10 to show the frame is false, explain the direction rule, and re-frame correctly.

cards.title: Building on framing means extending a single framed expression to a whole…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
Building on framing means extending a single framed expression to a whole situation: several quantities, one declared letter, and every other quantity EXPRESSED FROM the stated relation. The core relation is the sum-part: if two quantities add up to S and one of them is x, the other is S − x — a frame that rebuilds the partner from the poster at every value (x = 17 → 43; x = 25 → 35; the sum is S again and again). Three disciplines govern the building:
1. One poster, many relatives — but every relative must be DERIVED. "The sum of two numbers is 60" with one number x frames the other as 60 − x; "Ravi is 4 more than twice Meena" with Meena m frames Ravi as 2m + 4. A quantity that appears without a derivation is a smuggled letter — two independent quantities (pens and pencils, with no stated link) need two posters, never one.
2. Totals are gathered, not re-invented. The sum of the relatives is an expression like any page of this chapter: m + (2m + 4) gathers to 3m + 4, and s + (60 − s) gathers to 60 — the s-family cancelling itself (1 − 1 = 0). The tidy total then carries its coefficient and degree for reading (,).
3. The story gives the letter its RANGE. The page 60 − x works for every number x, but the STORY (two positive quantities summing to 60) only makes sense while 0 < x < 60 — at x = 70 the arithmetic runs on (60 − 70 = −10) but the story has died: a negative number of sweets, a negative age. A declared poster carries its story-range with it; frames are obedient, not sensible — sense is supplied by the situation.
The node's working tool is the case table: pick easy values inside the range, evaluate every relative and the total, and watch the relations hold row after row — the substitution echo run at scale, and the direct preparation for the evaluation-by-substitution work that closes the chapter.
steps: One declared letter plus one stated relation clothes an entire situation in algebra: every relative is derived from the poster, the total is gathered from the relatives, and the case table proves the relations hold at…
Argument 1 — the relation is a builder, not a label.
The last node framed single phrases; this node lets the page speak of MANY quantities while carrying ONE letter.

"Two numbers add to 60, one is x" builds the other as 60 − x — and the frame is not a description of one case, it is a MACHINE: feed x = 17 and it hands back 43; feed x = 40 and it hands back 20; every row keeps the…
The relation "sum is 60" was one sentence of English; the frame 60 − x is that sentence, ready to run at every value of the poster.
Argument 2 — comparison relations build the same way, with the last node's order discipline.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., x − 45 "since it is what remains", or 45 + x) reveals the sum-relation direction slip: x − 45 goes negative for every story-legal x (at x = 17 it gives −28, and 17 + (−28) = −11, not 45), and 45 + x overshoots the sum the story fixed …
remember: Two numbers add up to 45. Taking the smaller number as x, frame the larger number, and verify the frame at x = 17 and x = 25.
"Ravi is 5 years older than Meena." (a) Declare a letter and frame BOTH ages. (b) Frame the sum of their ages and gather it. (c) State the sum-frame's degree and name it by terms.
A student asks: "why is 45 − x a valid answer for 'the larger number' — shouldn't an answer be a NUMBER?" Explain what the frame 45 − x IS (what it gives, when), demonstrate with….

cards.title: A Maths Kit in the ICSE Class 6 Algebra curriculum is a structured set of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A Maths Kit in the ICSE Class 6 Algebra curriculum is a structured set of concrete manipulatives — typically algebra tiles (different colours/shapes for constants, variables, and their negatives), number cards, pattern blocks, and counters — designed to make abstract algebraic ideas tangible. The kit directly supports the chapter’s subtopics: it lets learners physically build and generalise patterns (e.g., odd numbers summing to n²), introduce unknowns through single‑operation contexts, and attach terminology (literal numbers, terms, coefficients, polynomials, degree, like/unlike terms) to visible pieces. By framing algebraic expressions with tiles, students see how a term like 3x is three “x‑tiles” and a constant 5 is five “unit tiles”. The kit also bridges to evaluating expressions by substituting a value for the variable (replacing each x‑tile with a given number of unit tiles) and to modelling linear equations in one variable (balancing tiles on two sides of a mat). It does not cover factorisation, quadratic expressions, or formal algebraic manipulation beyond the scope of Class 6.
steps: The Maths Kit turns invisible algebra into visible, touchable pieces so every learner can “see” the structure of an expression.
Here is why: concrete materials let children test ideas, make mistakes, and correct them without the pressure of abstract symbols.

Consider a classroom where each pair gets a set of tiles: small squares (units), rectangles (x), and large squares (x² — though x² is not used in Class 6, the large square can represent a “variable group” for extension).

First, the teacher revisits the pattern 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 using unit tiles arranged in L‑shapes; students notice each new odd number adds a layer, forming a perfect square — this is the n² generalisation.
Next, they introduce a red rectangle as “x” (the unknown).
A word problem: “Riya has some marbles; she gets 3 more and now has 7.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it represents the number 5”) reveals the misconception that every tile stands for a fixed numeric value rather than a placeholder for an unknown quantity.
remember: What does a single red rectangle tile typically represent in the Class 6 Maths Kit.
If a student places three blue unit tiles and two red rectangle tiles on the left side of the balance mat, which algebraic expression does this model.
A learner uses five unit tiles to represent the term 5x. Evaluate whether this representation is correct.

cards.title: Evaluating an expression by substitution means replacing the variable with a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
Evaluating an expression by substitution means replacing the variable with a definite number — one chosen member of the poster's family — and computing the resulting arithmetic. The discipline has three steps:
1. Replace every appearance. In 2x + 7 at x = 5, the single x becomes 5: 2 × 5 + 7. In 4xy + 2y − x at x = 2, y = 3, every letter gets ITS OWN declared value — x's value never serves for y (each poster is its own quantity, the chapter's two-posters discipline).
2. Compute in the anatomy's order: powers, then products, then sums. The exponent belongs to the LETTER alone: 4x² at x = 3 means 4 × (3 × 3) = 36 — the coefficient is not swept inside the square (4x² is four squares of side x, not one square of side 4x). Within a term, the coefficient multiplies the powered letter first; only then do whole terms (the katoris,) add and subtract: 2 × 5 + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17, never 2 × 12.
3. Read the output as one value of many. A substitution is a VISIT: the page keeps its poster, the machine stays mounted, and the next value runs a fresh meal — 3s + 7 at s = 5 gives 22, at s = 15 gives 52, and the expression is neither 22 nor 52 but the rule that produced both. Substituting x = 0 is the classic probe: it kills every term carrying x and leaves the constant standing (2n² − n + 6 at n = 0 gives 6), revealing the constant term as the machine's floor.
Substitution is the chapter's payoff ritual: it was the value-test behind framing, the case-table engine behind relations, and it is now the named skill the maths-kit work leads into — the act that turns every expression of this chapter into answers.
steps: Substitution feeds a chosen member of the variable's family into the expression-machine and runs the anatomy's arithmetic — replace everywhere, powers then products then sums — and the skill is complete when the two…
Argument 1 — the ritual completes the chapter's promise.
Every node of this chain built structure: terms (008), factors (010), coefficients (011), families (012), degree (013), like/unlike (014), framing (015), relations (016).
Substitution is where structure pays: the poster steps aside, a real number takes its place, and the page collapses to arithmetic the class has owned since Class 1.

The chapter's two-posters frame said the letter stands for ANY member of a family; substitution finally NAMES the member — and the machine answers for that one member while staying mounted for the next.

Argument 2 — order is not bureaucracy; it is the anatomy read aloud. 2x + 7 at x = 5 is TWO KATORIS: the literal term 2x fills first (2 × 5 = 10), the constant 7 already sits filled, and only then do the katoris pour…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3 × (6 + 4) = 30, or (3 + 6) + 4 = 13) reveals the read-it-like-a-sentence slip: the term 3x is ONE katori whose parts multiply together first, and the +4 pours in only afterwards — the page's term boundaries are the computation's…
remember: What is substitution? Evaluate 3x + 4 at x = 6, showing the replacement and the computation in order.
Evaluate: (a) 5n − 2 at n = 4; (b) 2k at k = 9. (c) Both machines happened to answer 18 — does that make the two expressions alike? State what each machine IS.
A student evaluates 2x + 7 at x = 5 as 2 × (5 + 7) =….

cards.title: Basic geometrical ideas in two dimensions form the vocabulary of plane geometry.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Basic geometrical ideas in two dimensions form the vocabulary of plane geometry. A point marks an exact location with no size. A line is a straight path extending infinitely in both directions; a line segment is the part of a line bounded by two distinct endpoints; a ray starts at one endpoint and continues infinitely in one direction. An angle is formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint called the vertex. Two lines in a plane that never intersect are parallel; two lines that intersect at a right angle (90°) are perpendicular. Reflection symmetry (or line symmetry) exists when a figure can be folded along a line so that the two halves coincide exactly; the fold line is the axis of symmetry. These concepts are interconnected: parallel and perpendicular relationships describe the relative position of lines; angles measure the turn between rays; symmetry uses the idea of a line as a mirror. In Class 6, students encounter these ideas through concrete models (geoboard, cardboard cut‑outs), drawings, and real‑life examples such as kolam patterns, window grills, and mirror reflections, building a foundation for later construction and measurement tasks.
steps: The big idea is that every flat shape you see around you — from a rangoli design to a window grill — is built from a few simple 2‑D geometrical objects: points, lines, line segments, rays, and angles, and many of these…
Here is why: (1) A point is like a tiny bindi on your forehead — it shows a precise spot but has no length or width.
(2) A line is like the straight edge of a long ruler that seems to go on forever in both directions; a line segment is the part of that ruler between the 0 cm and 15 cm marks.
(3) A ray is like a sunbeam that starts at the sun and travels outward endlessly.
(4) When two rays meet at a common point they form an angle; the corner of a book page is a right angle of 90°.
(5) Parallel lines are like the two long edges of a notebook — they stay the same distance apart and never meet.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "line segment") reveals the misconception that any straight drawing is a line segment, confusing the infinite nature of a line with the finite part students usually draw on paper.
remember: What is the geometrical term for a straight path that extends infinitely in both directions.
If two lines in a plane never meet, what are they called? Give an example from a classroom.
A student claims that a ray has two endpoints. Is this claim correct? Explain.

cards.title: Building on children’s previous learning in geometry means deliberately…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Building on children’s previous learning in geometry means deliberately activating the shape vocabulary, spatial reasoning, and informal symmetry ideas that students have gathered from everyday experiences and earlier classes. By Class 6, learners can usually name common two‑dimensional figures (circle, square, rectangle, triangle) and three‑dimensional solids (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, pyramid, prism). They have counted corners (vertices), edges, and faces on concrete models, and they have noticed mirror‑like patterns in rangoli, butterflies, or leaves.
