cards.title: The density activities are a station set in which the class runs the chapter's…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The density activities are a station set in which the class runs the chapter's density machinery ('s concept,'s process) on physical materials until the concept lives in the hands: (1) the equal-volume boxes — four identical 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm boxes filled with cotton, crumpled paper, water and sand; lifting them sorts the fillings by mass, and because the volumes are identical, the mass order IS the density order (1000 cm³ of each: cotton about 80 g, paper about 150 g, water 1000 g, sand about 1500 g) — the packing rate made liftable; (2) the fingerprint station — a regular aluminium block weighed and edge-measured, the three-step process executed end to end, 54 g ÷ 20 cm³ = 2.7 g/cm³ landing on the table; (3) the equal-volume cubes — 2 cm cubes of wood, aluminium, zinc and iron (4.8, 21.6, 56.8 and 62.4 g), ordered first by hand-feel and then by balance, the two rankings forced to agree; (4) the cut-in-half check — a plasticine block (36 cm³, 43.2 g, density 1.2) halved, each half re-weighed and re-measured (18 cm³, 21.6 g, still 1.2), the invariance law demonstrated with a knife; (5) the water-line sorting tray — materials predicted float-or-sink against 1 g/cm³, then dropped, every prediction graded by the tray. The shared design grammar is the area activities' grammar transplanted: predict first (a written guess column — which box is heaviest? floats or sinks?), measure with roles (lifter, weigher, measurer, checker), record everything (raw masses, dimensions, quotients with labels), and reconcile (hand-feel against balance, prediction against tray, whole against halves). The stations' product is a class that has personally felt 1.5 out-lift 0.08 at equal size, personally watched a quotient survive its own halving, and personally been wrong about a float — because density conviction built from lifting and dropping outlasts any number of stated rules.
steps: The density activities are the concept's gymnasium — identical boxes to lift, blocks to weigh and halve, predictions to drop into water — and every station converts one stated law of into an act the hands have performed.
Argument one: the equal-volume boxes make the packing rate a muscle memory.
Four identical boxes; the class lifts in sequence: the cotton box floats up, the paper box lifts easy, the water box pulls like a full bucket, the sand box thuds.

The guess sheet came first ("sand heaviest, everyone knows — but WHICH is second?"), and the surprise is the lesson: paper out-pulls cotton three-to-one at the same size, a fact the eye never suspected and the balance…

Then the arithmetic closes the trap: because the volumes are IDENTICAL, the masses rank in the same order as the densities — 80, 150, 1000, 1500 g become 0.08, 0.15, 1.0, 1.5 g/cm³ by one division each.

cards.title: The simple problems node is the chapter's drill hall…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The simple problems node is the chapter's drill hall: a graded set of numericals on density (D = M ÷ V with its rearrangements M = D × V and V = M ÷ D) and speed (S = D ÷ T with Distance = S × T and Time = D ÷ S), bound by one solving protocol that makes every problem the same four moves. The protocol: (1) WRITE the knowns — every given quantity with its unit, in a list; (2) NAME the mask — which quantity is missing decides the operation (density or speed missing → divide; mass or distance missing → multiply; volume or time missing → divide), the three-mask naming drilled in; (3) SUBSTITUTE — write the formula with the numbers in place BEFORE any arithmetic, units riding along; (4) CHECK by re-substitution — the answer re-enters its own equation and must rebuild a given quantity (2.7 g/cm³ × 160 cm³ must give back 432 g; 30 km/h × 0.6 h must give back 18 km). The grading ladder: one-step problems (one formula, one operation), two-step problems (compute volume then density; convert minutes to a fraction of an hour then divide), comparison problems (two movers or two materials ranked through computed rates), and mixed problems (both families on one scenario — a delivery whose load density and route speed interlock). The unit disciplines: density problems live in g and cm³ giving g/cm³; speed problems live in km and h giving km/h (or m and s giving m/s), with journey times in minutes converted to a fraction of an hour BEFORE any division (36 min = 36/60 = 3/5 h); no family conversions are required at this level (syllabus: units not required beyond these). The drill's product is not the answers — it is the reflex: a student who has run the four moves forty times stops guessing operations, stops dropping units, and starts hearing the check in their head before the teacher asks for it.
steps: The drill hall's promise: any density or speed problem this syllabus can set is the same four moves in different clothes — write the knowns, name the mask, substitute, check — and the ladder from one-step to mixed turns…
Argument one: naming the mask kills operation-guessing at the root.

Every problem in both families hides one of three masks: the RATE missing (density, speed — divide the total by the partner), the TOTAL missing (mass, distance — multiply rate by partner), or the PARTNER missing…

The first written line of every solution is the mask name — "find D", "find T" — because the mask decides everything downstream: a student who writes "T =?" cannot multiply by mistake, cannot divide upside down without…
The drill's first week refuses to accept any solution whose first line is arithmetic; the second week, the naming becomes silent and fast — the reflex installed.
Argument two: two-step problems are two masks in a trenchcoat, and the seam must show.
cards.misconception: a wrong answer with a complete protocol shows the fault at a fixable address (the mask, the conversion), while a right answer with no protocol proves nothing…
remember: State the four moves of the solving protocol, and explain why the check (re-substitution) is marked even when the answer is already right.

cards.title: The graduated cylinder in activities is the instrument at work…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The graduated cylinder in activities is the instrument at work: the precise reader of running the measurement load of the class's experiments, in four recurring roles. (1) MEASURING IN — supplying exact volumes to an experiment (25 mL of water into each group's beaker, 8 mL of ink into a dilution), read in and certified by the ritual (flat table, settled liquid, level eye, bottom of the meniscus). (2) DELIVERING BY DIFFERENCE — handing over a definite amount by the two-reading method: fill past the target, read (say 50 mL), pour out slowly to the target mark (25 mL), delivered = 50 − 25 = 25 mL — because pouring transfers approximately, but the cylinder's readings transfer exactly. (3) DISPLACEMENT WORK — finding small irregular solids' volumes by immersion: initial reading, solid lowered by thread, bubbles tapped, final reading; rise = volume (30 → 34 mL: a 4 cm³ marble; 50 → 55: a 5 cm³ key), the method of in daily use. (4) CARE AND VERIFICATION — the glass habits (carry upright by the base, never by the lip; no stirring with the cylinder; rinse between unlike liquids; check the scale against a known fill once a term), because a chipped, cracked or mis-read cylinder certifies nothing. The cylinder family itself is a ladder of precisions: a 10 mL cylinder (0.2 or 0.5 mL marks) for doses and small volumes, a 100 mL (1 mL marks) for ordinary class work, a 250 or 500 mL (2 or 5 mL marks) for bigger jobs — and choosing the rung is the same matching rule as ever: the finest marks must be comfortably smaller than the amount that matters. In the activity week's division of labour, the cylinder CERTIFIES while its wide partner, the beaker, CARRIES — the full partnership is the closing business of.

cards.title: The graduated beaker in activities is the bulk partner of the class's liquid…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The graduated beaker in activities is the bulk partner of the class's liquid work: a wide, sturdy vessel with coarse graduations (25 or 50 mL steps on a 250 mL beaker) whose jobs are CARRYING (fetching and holding the session's water supply), PREPARING (mixing solutions — 250 mL of water plus 5 g of salt, stirred with a rod, warmed if the method allows), HEATING (the vessel designed to stand on a flame or hot plate with a wire grid — a role the cylinder is never given), and ROUGH MEASURING (reading "about 200 mL" against its marks, honest to the nearest step or so, never to the millilitre). Its certification limit is geometry, not quality: the wide cross-section that makes it stable, stirrable and heatable is the same width that makes small volumes move its level invisibly, so fine marks on a beaker would certify nothing — the coarseness is the honesty (the argument of, lived daily). The coordination protocol runs every experiment: the beaker fetches and holds the bulk ("fill me to about the 250 mark"), the cylinder measures and certifies the exact part ("take 50 mL of that, by the ritual"), and the record names which instrument vouched for which number ("about 250 mL carried; 50.0 mL certified"). This node also closes the chapter: the instrument shelf is now complete — scale (length), graph paper (area, regular and irregular), balance (mass), clock/stopwatch (time), cylinder (exact liquid volumes and displacements), beaker (bulk liquid work) — and every quantity the chapter promised (area, volume, density, speed) has its unit, its instrument, its reading discipline, and its problem protocol. The chapter's through-line, restated as the beaker-and-cylinder handshake it has been all along: rough tools carry, precise tools certify, and a measurement is honest when the record says which is which.
steps: The graduated beaker is the chapter's last instrument and its strongest hand — carrying, preparing, heating and rough-measuring while the cylinder certifies — and the partnership it seals doubles as the chapter's own…

PREPARE: the solution station lives in the beaker — 250 mL of water read "about", 5 g of salt from the balance, the rod stirring freely in the wide belly (the cylinder's own wall could never host a rod); the discipline…

HEAT: only the beaker goes near the flame, on a wire grid, a third-full at most, supervised — because its thick, open, stable body is built for it; the discipline is the boundary sentence: "the cylinder never heats…
Argument two: honest coarse reading is the beaker's form of the ritual.
